# From Sampling to Efficient Estimation {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-reduction"}

<span id="functions-and-inputs"></span>

Keep $\mu=\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(\vX)]$ fixed, while changing how we compute it

| Inputs | Output | Role |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $\vX\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$ | $f(\vX)$ | Target output |
| $\vZ=\vS(\vU)\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ | $g(\vZ)$ | Alternative contribution |
| $\vU\sim\Unif[0,1]^d$ | $h(\vU)=g\bigl(\vS(\vU)\bigr)$ | Complete calculation from uniforms |

$$
\mu=\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(\vX)]
=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}[g(\vZ)]
=\Ex_{\Unif[0,1]^d}[h(\vU)]
=\int_{[0,1]^d}h(\vu)\,\dif\vu
$$

- Change the [contribution]{.alert}: replace $f(\vX)$ by an equal-mean $g(\vZ)$
- Change the [point design]{.alert}: arrange uniform inputs before evaluating $h$

::: {.key-point}
Equal means [do not imply]{.alert} $g(\vZ)\stackrel d=f(\vX)$

Exact transport [implies]{.alert} $h(\vU) \stackrel d=g(\vZ)$
:::

::: {.notes}
The equality concerns expectations, not equality of individual outputs or
output distributions. An alternative contribution may include importance
weights, controls, or a conditional expectation. The self-normalized IS
subsection later introduces a ratio estimator as a separate extension, not
a fixed equal-mean contribution average. Its sampling law belongs
with g. Exact transport is a useful case where the output distributions
agree: if T(Z) has the target law and g=f composed with T, then g(Z) and
f(X) have the same distribution. Other equal-mean contributions may change
the distribution and variance. The function h includes that contribution and all transforms from
the uniform input. If the input is already uniform, S is the identity and
h=g. Different constructions may require different cube dimensions.
Use h_f=f composed with T and h_g=g composed with S when comparing two
representations; generic h avoids carrying that subscript through every
QMC or RQMC formula. Low discrepancy sampling places its points on the unit
cube, which explains the switch from g to h in those formulas.
:::

---

### Recall the sampling paths

$\vU\sim\Unif[0,1]^d,\quad \vZ\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}},\quad
\vX\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$

- [Generating Samples: transport]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#transport-maps): $\vZ=\vS(\vU)$, then $\vX=\vT(\vZ)$
- [Generating Samples: acceptance–rejection]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#acceptancerejection-sampling): retain selected proposals as $\vX$
- [Markov Chain Monte Carlo]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#the-metropolishastings-algorithm): propose $\vZ_i\mid\vX_i$; accept or repeat $\vX_i$; target law at stationarity

For a direct target transport $\vX=\vT(\vU)$ use $h_f=f\circ\vT$<br>
For the alternative $\vZ=\vS(\vU)$ use $h_g=g\circ\vS$

::: {.key-point}
Write $h$ for either complete [unit-cube integrand]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
Here the direct target map T includes the proposal-generation map when
needed. The first bullet shows the more general composition T(S(U)) used
in Generating Samples. Acceptance–rejection and MCMC have additional
selection or history structure; this recap does not assert IID target
outputs from those constructions or a fixed d-input formula for a whole
rejection or Markov-chain run.
:::

## Variance and variation reduction {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-reduction"}

Keep the [target]{.alert} quantity, but change its computational representation:

\begin{gather*}
\vX\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}},\quad Y=f(\vX),\qquad
\vZ\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}},\quad Y_g=g(\vZ) \\
 \alerttext{And} \quad \mu=\Ex(Y) = \Ex(Y_g)
\end{gather*}

Two sample means estimate the same $\mu$:

\begin{align*}
\hmu_{f,n}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(\vX_i),&
\hmu_{g,n}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}g(\vZ_i)
\end{align*}

- Change the function, the sampling distribution, or both
- Seek lower error for comparable computational [work]{.alert}
- Changing only the function gives the special case $g(\vX)$
- Label contributions by method: $Y_{\mathrm{IS}}$, $Y_{\mathrm{CV}}$, $Y_{\mathrm{CMC}}$

---

### Variance reduction

For IID samples and finite second moments, both sample means are unbiased:

\begin{align*}
\var(\hmu_{f,n})&=\frac{\var_{\mathrm{tar}}\{f(\vX)\}}n,&
\var(\hmu_{g,n})&=\frac{\var_{\mathrm{prop}}\{g(\vZ)\}}n
\end{align*}

Their MSEs equal their variances; IID RMSE is [$\Order(n^{-1/2})$]{.alert}

::: {.key-point}
Equal [means]{.alert} allow different output distributions and different [variances]{.alert}
:::

For [randomized]{.alert} low discrepancy inputs, dependence [changes]{.alert} the variance formula

::: {.notes}
The two methods need not be independent of one another for these individual
variance formulas. Each method needs independent replicates internally.
Compare computational costs as well as the variance of one contribution.
Introduction showed that accepting some bias can reduce MSE; here we compare
unbiased estimators. Degenerate zero-variance cases need no asymptotic rate.
:::

---

### Variation reduction for low discrepancy sampling

To compare designs on the unit cube, make the uniform inputs explicit:

\begin{align*}
\vX&=\vT(\vU),& h_f(\vu)&=f\bigl(\vT(\vu)\bigr),\\
\vZ&=\vS(\vU),& h_g(\vu)&=g\bigl(\vS(\vu)\bigr)
\end{align*}

Both cube integrands have integral $\mu$; keep the nodes $\vu_0,\ldots,\vu_{n-1}$ fixed

For equal-weight averages in a space containing constants use the
[sharper variation]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#variation-ignores-constants)

$$
\operatorname{vtn}_K(h)=\min_{c\in\reals}\norm{h-c}_{\mathcal H_K}
$$

$$
\left|\mu-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}h_g(\vu_i)\right|
\le D\bigl(F_{\mathrm{unif}},\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K\bigr)\operatorname{vtn}_K(h_g)
$$

- Nodes determine [discrepancy]{.alert}; the composed cube integrand determines [variation]{.alert}
- Seek smaller $\operatorname{vtn}_K(h_g)$ for the same nodes and kernel

::: {.notes}
The notation $\vT$ identifies a transport from uniform inputs to the target;
$\vS$ generates proposal draws. Neither map must be displayed when uniform
inputs are incidental. This common-cube comparison assumes compatible input
dimensions; conditioning can reduce dimension.
The bound is the Markov Chain Monte Carlo worst-case integration-error bound.
For sufficiently smooth composed cube integrands, nested uniform scrambling
gives variance nearly $\Order(n^{-3})$ and RMSE nearly $\Order(n^{-3/2})$.
This is not a guarantee for every randomization or integrand.
[Owen (1997)]({{< meta papers.owen_1997_scrambled_net_variance.doi_url >}})
provides the variance result.
:::

---

### The Keister example

Write the original integral as a [target expectation]{.alert}:

\begin{gather*}
\mu=\int_{\reals^d}\cos(\norm{\vx})\me^{-\norm{\vx}^2}\,\dif\vx
=\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(\vX)],\\
\vX\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mI_d/2),\qquad
f(\vx)=\mpi^{d/2}\cos(\norm{\vx})
\end{gather*}

Choose $\vZ_a\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mI_d/a^2)$ and apply a [density correction]{.alert}:

$$
g_a(\vz)=\frac{(2\mpi)^{d/2}}{a^d}
\cos(\norm{\vz})\exp\bigl[-(1-a^2/2)\norm{\vz}^2\bigr]
$$

Every $a>0$ gives $\Ex[g_a(\vZ_a)]=\mu$; changing $a$ changes the contribution

::: {.notes}
First identify a probability density in the original integral. Here
$\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)=\mpi^{-d/2}\me^{-\norm{\vx}^2}$ is the
$\Norm(\vzero,\mI_d/2)$ density, so
$\me^{-\norm{\vx}^2}=\mpi^{d/2}\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)$.
The factor $\mpi^{d/2}$ belongs in $f$ when the integral is written as
$\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(\vX)]$.
:::

---

### Keister on the unit cube

Set $\vS_a(\vu)=\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(u_j)/a\bigr)_{j=1}^d$ and
$h_a(\vu)=g_a\bigl(\vS_a(\vu)\bigr)$

With $\vq(\vu)=\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(u_j)\bigr)_{j=1}^d$,

$$
h_a(\vu)=\frac{(2\mpi)^{d/2}}{a^d}
\cos\bigl(\norm{\vq(\vu)}/a\bigr)
\exp\bigl[-(2-a^2)\norm{\vq(\vu)}^2/(2a^2)\bigr]
$$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Verify $g_a=f\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}/\varrho_{\mathrm{prop},a}$ and
$\int_{[0,1]^d}h_a(\vu)\,\dif\vu=\mu$</span>
:::

- $0<a^2\le2$: $h_a$ is [bounded]{.alert}; $a=\sqrt2$ gives $g_a=f$
- $2<a^2<4$: $h_a$ is [unbounded]{.alert} but has [finite]{.alert} variance, including $a=1.6$
- $a^2\ge4$: [infinite]{.alert} variance

Choose $a$ by estimator variance or cube-integrand variation

::: {.notes}
Every positive $a$ preserves the mean. The second moment is
$$
\Ex[g_a(\vZ_a)^2]=\frac{(2\mpi)^{d/2}}{a^d}
\int_{\reals^d}\cos^2(\norm{\vz})
\exp\bigl[-(2-a^2/2)\norm{\vz}^2\bigr]\,\dif\vz.
$$
It is finite precisely when $a^2<4$. For $2<a^2<4$, the cube-boundary
singularity is mild enough for square integrability. At $a^2=4$, Gaussian
decay disappears and the squared cosine cannot provide cancellation;
for larger $a^2$, the envelope grows. The notebook uses $a=1.6$ to explore
an unbounded integrand that still has finite variance.
:::

[Explore $a$ in the Keister notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/applications/KeisterExample.ipynb)

## Transforming an integral {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="analysis-importance"}

Start with $\displaystyle \mu=\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(\vX)]=\int_{\mathcal X}f(\vx)\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)\,\dif\vx$

Choose an [invertible]{.alert} differentiable map $\vT:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X$
and $\vZ\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ covering the required support

\begin{align*}
g(\vz)&=f\bigl(\vT(\vz)\bigr)w_T(\vz),\\
w_T(\vz)&=
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\bigl(\vT(\vz)\bigr)
\left|\det\nabla\vT(\vz)\right|}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)}
\end{align*}

Then $\mu=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}[g(\vZ)]$, where $\nabla\vT(\vz)$ is the [Jacobian]{.alert} matrix
of $\vT$ and $\left|\det\nabla\vT(\vz)\right|$ is its volume-scaling factor

::: {.key-point}
A general change of variables preserves the integral through a correction [weight]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
Assume the map and inverse meet the change-of-variables theorem's conditions,
and the proposal is positive wherever the transformed integrand is nonzero.
The target density is normalized; integrability is required for the expectation.
The transformed proposal need not have the specified target density.
For a Lebesgue integral $\int r(\vx)\,\dif\vx$, the same mechanism gives
$g(\vz)=r(\vT(\vz))|\det\nabla\vT(\vz)|/
\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)$ without introducing a target density.
:::

---

### Transforming a random variable

An [exact transport]{.alert} $\vT:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X$ satisfies

$$
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\bigl(\vT(\vz)\bigr)
\left|\det\nabla\vT(\vz)\right|
=\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)
$$

Then $w_T(\vz)=1$ wherever $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)>0$, and so
$\vX=\vT(\vZ)\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$, and

$$
g(\vz)=f\bigl(\vT(\vz)\bigr),\qquad
g(\vZ)\stackrel d=f(\vX)
$$

::: {.key-point}
Exact transport preserves the whole output [distribution]{.alert}, including IID variance
:::

- Provides access to target samples; construction and evaluation costs can differ
- Different transports can change low discrepancy performance through the cube integrand

---

### Exact transport makes importance weights constant

| Choice of map | Correction | Alternative contribution |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Exact transport $\vT$ | $w_T(\vz)=1$ | $f\bigl(\vT(\vZ)\bigr)$ |
| Identity map  $\vT(\vz)=\vz$ <br>(importance sampling)| $w(\vz)=\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vz)/\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)$ | $f(\vZ)w(\vZ)$ |

::: {.key-point}
Exact transport changes [samples]{.alert}; importance sampling changes [contributions]{.alert}

Same expectation $\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(\vX)]=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}[g(\vZ)]=\mu$

[but]{.alert}
output distributions and variances may differ (want them to)
:::

## Importance sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="importance-sampling"}

Choose $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}>0$ wherever $f\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\ne0$

\begin{align*}
w(\vz)&=\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vz)}{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)},&
g_{\mathrm{IS}}(\vz)&=f(\vz)w(\vz),\\
\mu&=\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(\vX)]
=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}[g_{\mathrm{IS}}(\vZ)]
\end{align*}

For $\vZ_0,\ldots,\vZ_{n-1}\ \IIDsim\ \varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$,

$$
Y_{\mathrm{IS}}=g_{\mathrm{IS}}(\vZ)=f(\vZ)w(\vZ),\qquad \Ex(Y_{\mathrm{IS}})=\mu
$$

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{IS},n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}Y_{\mathrm{IS},i}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(\vZ_i)w(\vZ_i)
$$

$w$ is the [weight]{.alert} function; $W=w(\vZ)$ is its random value

---

### One proposal, three unbiased estimators {#one-proposal-two-unbiased-estimators}

\begin{gather*}
\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)=1,\qquad
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)=2x,\qquad 0<x,z<1,\\
Z_0,\ldots,Z_{n-1}\ \IIDsim\ \Unif(0,1),\qquad
\mu=\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(X)]
\end{gather*}

| | Exact transport | Importance sampling | [Acceptance–rejection]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#the-same-target-by-acceptancerejection) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Construction | $T(z)=\sqrt z$ | $w(z)=2z$ | Accept $X=Z$ if $V\le Z$ |
| Contribution | $f(\sqrt Z)$ | $2Zf(Z)$ | $f(X)$ for accepted $X$ |
| Estimator | $\displaystyle\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(\sqrt{Z_i})$ | $\displaystyle\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2Z_if(Z_i)$ | $\displaystyle\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(X_i)$ |
| Output distribution | Same as $Y=f(X)$ | Generally different from $Y$ | Same as $Y=f(X)$ |
| Proposal cost | $n$ | $n$ | Average $2n$ for $n$ accepted |

Acceptance–rejection: independent $V\sim\Unif(0,1)$ for each proposal; continue until $n$ accepted points $X_0,\ldots,X_{n-1}$

::: {.notes}
All three estimates are unbiased for the same target expectation when $f$ is
integrable. The acceptance–rejection column links to the matching triangular
target example in Generating Samples. Its envelope constant is $M=2$, so the
acceptance probability is $1/2$. Accepted points are indexed separately from
the proposal stream; continue drawing fresh independent proposal/decision
pairs until exactly $n$ acceptances have been collected. The number of
proposals is random, with mean $2n$. The other two columns use exactly $n$
proposals. Thus equal numbers of averaged contributions do not mean equal
proposal costs. Each rejection attempt also requires an independent decision
uniform $V$. The acceptance–rejection estimator here averages a fixed number
of accepted points, not a random number obtained from a fixed proposal budget.
:::

---

### Seeing the contribution variances

```{python}
#| label: importance-contributions
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Two plots overlay exact-transport contributions g_ET(Z)=f(sqrt(Z)) in blue and importance contributions g_IS(Z)=2Zf(Z) in orange, using the same uniform input Z, one plot for each function. For f(x)=x, importance sampling spreads outputs more widely; for f(x)=1-x, it concentrates them more tightly around their common mean. Markers indicate equally spaced uniform input quantiles."
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-format: svg
#| out-width: 94%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "stix"
importance_grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 501)
importance_quantiles = (np.arange(20) + 0.5) / 20
fig_importance, axes_importance = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.6), constrained_layout=True
)
importance_cases = [
    (lambda t: t, lambda t: 2*t**2, 2/3,
     r"$f(x)=x$", r"$g_{\mathrm{IS}}(z)=2z^2$", "16/45", 2.05),
    (lambda t: 1-t, lambda t: 2*t*(1-t), 1/3,
     r"$f(x)=1-x$", r"$g_{\mathrm{IS}}(z)=2z(1-z)$", "1/45", 1.05),
]
for ax, (target_f, importance_g, mean, f_label, g_label, is_var, ymax) in zip(axes_importance, importance_cases):
    for function, points, label, variance, color, marker in [
        (lambda z: target_f(np.sqrt(z)), importance_quantiles, r"$g_{\mathrm{ET}}(z)=\sqrt{z}$" if mean > 0.5 else r"$g_{\mathrm{ET}}(z)=1-\sqrt{z}$", "1/18", "#1f5a91", "o"),
        (importance_g, importance_quantiles, g_label, is_var, "#bd5d15", "s"),
    ]:
        values = function(points)
        ax.plot(importance_grid, function(importance_grid), color=color, lw=2.6,
                label=label + r"; $\mathrm{var}=" + variance + "$")
        ax.vlines(points, mean, values, color=color, alpha=0.16, lw=1.1)
        ax.scatter(points, values, color=color, marker=marker, s=24, zorder=3)
    ax.axhline(mean, color="#666666", ls="--", lw=1.4,
               label=r"Common mean $\mu=" + ("2/3" if mean > 0.5 else "1/3") + "$")
    ax.set_title(f_label, fontsize=23)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"Uniform input $z$", fontsize=19)
    ax.set_ylabel("Contribution", fontsize=19)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.045*ymax, ymax)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=14)
    ax.legend(loc="upper left" if mean > 0.5 else "upper right", fontsize=16,
              framealpha=0.95)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.12)
plt.show()
```

$g_{\mathrm{ET}}(z)=f(\sqrt z)$; $g_{\mathrm{IS}}(z)=2zf(z)$; both use $Z\sim\Unif(0,1)$

Markers: equally probable input quantiles; dashed line: common mean

::: {.notes}
The dots are deterministic quantile illustrations, not a random Monte Carlo sample.
For each curve, each marker represents the midpoint of a probability bin of mass 1/20.
Both curves use the same uniform input points (i+1/2)/20.
Vertical segments show deviations from the mean. Since both inputs are uniform,
variance is the integral of the squared vertical deviations.
The two curves in each plot share the same axes.
For f(x)=x, importance sampling increases contribution variance by a factor 6.4.
For f(x)=1-x, it reduces contribution variance by a factor 2.5.
The exact-transport output f(sqrt(Z)) has the same distribution as f(X),
so the blue curves also represent the target-output variance.
:::

---

### Compare transport and importance sampling

$Z\sim\Unif(0,1)$; target density $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)=2x$ on $(0,1)$

\begin{align*}
Y_T&=f(\sqrt Z),&Y_{\mathrm{IS}}&=2Zf(Z)
\end{align*}

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Compare the two contributions
<span class="exsub">For $f(x)=x$, compute their means and variances</span>
<span class="exsub">Repeat for $f(x)=1-x$</span>
<span class="exsub">Explain why the variance ranking reverses</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
For f(x)=x, both means are 2/3; the transport variance is 1/18 and
the IS variance is 16/45. For f(x)=1-x, both means are 1/3; the
transport variance remains 1/18 and the IS variance is 1/45.
Compute each variance as its second moment minus the squared mean.
The contribution's shape, not the target density alone, determines the
variance. In the second case, the factor 2Z partly offsets the decrease
in 1-Z. The next slide collects the results. These compare equal numbers
of contributions, without claiming equal computational cost.
:::

---

### Variance depends on the function

- Displayed variances: [one]{.alert} estimator contribution
- Sample-mean variances: [divide]{.alert} by $n$

| $f(x)$ | $\mu$ | Transport: $\var[f(\sqrt Z)]$ | Importance sampling: $\var[2Zf(Z)]$ | Smaller |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| $x$ | $2/3$ | $1/18$ | $16/45$ | transport |
| $1-x$ | $1/3$ | $1/18$ | $1/45$ | importance sampling |

::: {.key-point}
[No]{.alert} universal variance winner

Target samples support ordinary averages for every $f$

Weighted proposals can be [better]{.alert} or [worse]{.alert} for a particular $f$
:::

---

### Brownian motion with drift

Let $\vX\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mSigma)$ be the target Brownian path, with
$\Sigma_{jk}=\min(t_j,t_k)$ and discounted payoff $Y=f(\vX)$

Choose $\vZ\sim\Norm(\va,\mSigma)$, where
$\va=\theta(t_1,\ldots,t_d)^\mathsf T$

\begin{align*}
w(\vz)&=\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vz)}{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)}
=\exp\!\left(-\theta z_d+\frac{\theta^2t_d}{2}\right),\\
Y_{\mathrm{IS}}&=g_{\mathrm{IS}}(\vZ)=f(\vZ)w(\vZ),\qquad \Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}[Y_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\mu
\end{align*}

- Drift makes positive payoffs [more common]{.alert}
- Weights [preserve]{.alert} the target expectation; a good drift can reduce variance

[Asian option variance-reduction notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/performance/AsianOptionVarianceReduction.ipynb)

## Self-normalized importance sampling {#self-normalized-importance-sampling .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="importance-sampling"}

Suppose the [target normalizer]{.alert} is unknown

\begin{align*}
C_{\mathrm{tar}}&=\int\widetilde\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)\,\dif\vx,&
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)&=\frac{\widetilde\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)}{C_{\mathrm{tar}}}
\end{align*}

For $\vZ_0,\ldots,\vZ_{n-1}\ \IIDsim\ \varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$, use

$$
\widetilde w(\vz)=\frac{\widetilde\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vz)}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)}=C_{\mathrm{tar}}w(\vz)
$$

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{SN},n}
=\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(\vZ_i)\widetilde w(\vZ_i)}
       {\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\widetilde w(\vZ_i)}
$$

- Any common positive weight multiplier [cancels]{.alert}
- Require proposal coverage of the target support and a [positive denominator]{.alert}

::: {.key-point}
A [ratio of sample averages]{.alert} handles the unknown normalization
:::

::: {.notes}
Owen, Section 9.2, calls this self-normalized importance sampling; the same
ratio appears in equation (11.27). Assume 0<C_tar<infinity, IID proposal
draws, full target-support coverage up to null sets, and integrability of f
under the target. Unlike ordinary IS for a single integrand, the denominator
requires coverage even where f is zero but the target density is positive.
The denominator can be zero at finite n when every proposed weight is zero;
the estimator is defined only when it is positive.

The proposal is normalized in the visible formula. If only an unnormalized
proposal is evaluable but sampling from its normalized law is available,
use tilde_varrho_tar/tilde_varrho_prop instead. The resulting weights differ
by a common positive constant, which also cancels. Self-normalization estimates
a normalized expectation, not the unnormalized integral of f times the target.

When the normalized density ratio is computable, ordinary IS remains available
and is unbiased for integrable f. Both individual normalizers need not be
known: a known ratio suffices. Self-normalization is still an option, with
different finite-sample properties; neither estimator universally dominates.
This ratio method belongs to IS, independently of MCMC, and does not turn
proposal draws into target draws.
:::

---

### Posterior means by likelihood weighting {#posterior-means-by-likelihood-weighting}

Recall [Bayes' theorem]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#bayesian-inference) with likelihood $L(\theta;y_{\mathrm{obs}})$ and prior density $\varrho_{\mathrm{prior}}$

$$
\mu_{\mathrm{post}}=\Ex(\Theta\mid y_{\mathrm{obs}})
=\frac{\int\theta L(\theta;y_{\mathrm{obs}})\varrho_{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta)\,\dif\theta}
       {\int L(\theta;y_{\mathrm{obs}})\varrho_{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta)\,\dif\theta}
$$

Draw $Z_i\ \IIDsim\ \varrho_{\mathrm{prior}}$ and use [likelihood weights]{.alert}

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{post},n}
=\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}Z_iL(Z_i;y_{\mathrm{obs}})}
       {\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}L(Z_i;y_{\mathrm{obs}})}
$$

- The unknown evidence $\varrho_D(y_{\mathrm{obs}})$ [cancels]{.alert}
- A posterior concentrated in a small part of the prior can make weights very uneven

::: {.key-point}
Prior proposals with likelihood weighting give [self-normalized IS]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
This uses the same likelihood, prior, posterior, and evidence notation as
the Bayesian-inference slide in Markov Chain Monte Carlo. Here the proposal
is the prior, so the unnormalized target is
tilde_varrho_tar(theta)=L(theta;y_obs)varrho_prior(theta), the target
normalizer C_tar is the evidence varrho_D(y_obs), and the unnormalized
importance weight is just L(theta;y_obs). The proposal draws are named Z_i
to preserve their role; their distribution is the prior, not the posterior.
Require finite positive evidence, an integrable posterior first moment,
and a positive sample denominator. The same construction estimates any
integrable posterior expectation by replacing Z_i in the numerator by f(Z_i).

The exact posterior mean is a ratio of integrals. The displayed numerical
estimator is self-normalized IS because it estimates those integrals using
prior proposals. It is generally biased at finite n and consistent under
the preceding assumptions. If IID posterior draws are available instead,
their ordinary sample mean is unbiased for the posterior mean. An ordinary
average of MCMC posterior states is a different estimator too; it does not
become self-normalized IS merely because its target is a posterior.

For a two-point illustration, take prior probabilities 1/2,1/2 on theta=0,1
and likelihood values 1,3. The posterior probabilities are 1/4,3/4, giving
posterior mean 3/4. With one prior proposal the likelihood cancels, so the
displayed estimate has expectation 1/2. This makes the finite-sample bias
concrete without requiring any MCMC construction. A better proposal can
help when prior proposals rarely reach the concentrated posterior.
:::

---

### Bias and consistency {#self-normalization-bias-and-consistency}

Two sample averages estimate two integrals

\begin{align*}
\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(\vZ_i)\widetilde w(\vZ_i)
&\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathrm{a.s.}}C_{\mathrm{tar}}\mu\\
\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\widetilde w(\vZ_i)
&\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathrm{a.s.}}C_{\mathrm{tar}}>0
\end{align*}

Hence $\hmu_{\mathrm{SN},n}\to\mu$ almost surely under the stated conditions

- [Generally biased]{.alert} at finite $n$: unbiased components do not imply an unbiased ratio
- [Exact for constants]{.alert}: $f\equiv c$ gives $\hmu_{\mathrm{SN},n}=c$
- A ratio estimator needs its own [bias and variance]{.alert} analysis

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Target density $2x$ on $(0,1)$, uniform proposal, and $f(x)=x$
<span class="exsub">For $n=1$, simplify $\hmu_{\mathrm{SN},1}$ and compare its expectation with $\mu$</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The strong law applies separately to the numerator and denominator sample
averages; their limits are C_tar times mu and C_tar. The ratio then converges
almost surely. Positive C_tar makes the sample denominator eventually positive
almost surely, though an initial finite sample can have zero denominator.

For the exercise, tilde_varrho_tar(x)=x is enough, so tilde_w(z)=z. A uniform
proposal lies in (0,1) almost surely and its weight is positive. With n=1,
the weight cancels and the estimate is Z_0. Its expectation is 1/2, whereas
the target mean is 2/3; the bias is -1/6. More observations give consistency,
not a claim of exact finite-sample unbiasedness or a universal variance gain.

The sample-normalized weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so the estimate
is a weighted average of the observed f values and integrates constants exactly.
Statements about finite-sample bias assume the estimator's expectation exists.
When the relevant moments exist, MSE = variance + bias squared. The earlier
equal-mean IID contribution formulas and their variance-only cost comparison
do not apply automatically to this ratio estimator. No confidence interval or
stopping rule for the ratio is asserted here.
:::

---

### Acceptance–rejection with a fixed proposal budget {#acceptance-rejection-with-a-fixed-proposal-budget}

Use independent proposals and a fixed valid envelope<br>
Let $I_i$ indicate acceptance and $K_N=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}I_i$

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{AR},N}
=\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}I_i f(\vZ_i)}{K_N},\qquad K_N>0
$$

This is normalization by a sample total, with [zero–one weights]{.alert}

| Stopping rule | Accepted-sample average |
|:---|:---|
| Fix $n$ acceptances | Unbiased average of $n$ IID target draws |
| Fix $N$ proposals | Unbiased conditional on $K_N>0$ |

If $K_N=0$, the ratio is undefined

::: {.key-point}
A random denominator does [not by itself imply bias]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
Let tilde_w=tilde_varrho_tar/varrho_prop, and use a known fixed envelope
M >= sup tilde_w with independent uniform decisions. Then
Prob(I_i=1 | Z_i)=tilde_w(Z_i)/M and the unconditional acceptance probability
is a=C_tar/M. Assume 0<a<=1 and integrable f under the target. Conditional
on any specified acceptance pattern, the accepted proposals are independent
and each has the normalized target law. Therefore, for every k>0,
E(hatmu_AR,N | K_N=k)=mu, and E(hatmu_AR,N | K_N>0)=mu.
This conditional unbiasedness is a special property of rejection sampling,
so random sample count alone does not establish ratio-estimator bias.

Here K_N is binomial(N,a), so Prob(K_N=0)=(1-a)^N. The ratio itself is
undefined on that event. If an implementation returns a fixed value b
when no proposal is accepted, its unconditional bias is
(b-mu)(1-a)^N. For zero fill this is -mu(1-a)^N. Discarding an empty batch
and trying again gives the conditional unbiased average, but then the
overall proposal count is random. Fixing the number n of accepted draws
also gives an unbiased target average, with a random proposal count.

The connection to ordinary self-normalized IS is algebraic: replacing each
acceptance indicator I_i by its conditional mean tilde_w(Z_i)/M in both
sums gives the self-normalized importance ratio. The ratio of conditional
expectations is not generally the conditional expectation of the ratio.
Do not infer a Rao–Blackwell variance inequality or exact unbiasedness for
SNIS from that replacement. In particular, the one-proposal bias example
on the preceding slides remains valid.

Owen, Section 9.5, writes the fixed-proposal rejection-sampling average as
a ratio with a random number of acceptances. Keep the zero-acceptance event
explicit when comparing it with self-normalized IS. The fixed-envelope and
independence assumptions matter; no adaptive rejection scheme is claimed here.
:::

---

### Exact transport with an unknown target normalizer {#transport-with-unknown-normalizer}

Target density $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}=\widetilde\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}/C_{\mathrm{tar}}$ with [unknown]{.alert} $C_{\mathrm{tar}}$

Draw $\vZ_i\overset{\mathrm{IID}}{\sim}\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ from a normalized source<br>
An [exact transport]{.alert} $\vT$ gives $\vT(\vZ_i)\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$

For an invertible differentiable $\vT$, the weights are constant

$$
\widetilde w_T(\vz)=
\frac{\widetilde\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\bigl(\vT(\vz)\bigr)
\left|\det\nabla\vT(\vz)\right|}{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)}
=C_{\mathrm{tar}}
$$

The unknown constant cancels

\begin{align*}
\hmu_{\mathrm{SN},T,n}
&=\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f\bigl(\vT(\vZ_i)\bigr)\widetilde w_T(\vZ_i)}
       {\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\widetilde w_T(\vZ_i)}\\
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f\bigl(\vT(\vZ_i)\bigr)
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
An exact map generates [target samples]{.alert} without separately knowing $C_{\mathrm{tar}}$
:::

::: {.notes}
The source/proposal density is normalized. Only the target normalizing
constant is unknown. Throughout the visible slide, T is an exact transport
from the source to the normalized target, not an approximate fitted map.
The exact map encodes normalization; constructing it can be difficult.

This follows directly from the earlier change-of-variables formula: the
normalized transport correction is w_T=1, so the unnormalized correction
is C_tar. Both sums contain the same factor C_tar. Integrable f and IID
source draws therefore give an ordinary unbiased target average in this
constant-weight case. General nonconstant-weight self-normalization is
generally biased at finite n.

The existing triangular example works without supplying the target normalizer
as a separate input. With tilde_varrho_tar(x)=x on (0,1), a uniform source,
and T(z)=sqrt(z), the unnormalized correction is
sqrt(z)/(2 sqrt(z))=1/2, which equals C_tar. In contrast, the identity map
has tilde_w(z)=z and gives the nonconstant-weight ratio from the preceding
exercise. An arbitrary positive multiplier on the target shape changes only
the common correction constant, not the normalized distribution or exact map.

For a general one-dimensional target, the quantile map uses the ratio of
the cumulative integral of tilde_varrho to its total integral. That ratio
is insensitive to an arbitrary density scale, but computing and inverting
it can still require difficult global information. In higher dimensions,
maps can be fitted against an unnormalized target without separately computing
its normalizer. An approximate map need not produce exact target draws.
A fitted flow generally approximates the target; exactness
must not be inferred merely from calling the map a transport or normalizing
flow. Importance weighting or Metropolis correction can address the mismatch,
with the appropriate finite-sample qualifications.

Supporting reference: [Marzouk, Moselhy, Parno, and Spantini, Sections 3.1--3.3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.05023).
The existence and the practical construction of an exact transport are
different questions. Keep this clarification here in Improving Efficiency;
it does not require reopening Generating Samples or Markov Chain Monte Carlo.
:::


---

### Weighted empirical distributions {#weighted-empirical-distributions}

Same IID proposal points, different masses: approximate the [target]{.alert} by reweighting

\begin{align*}
\widehat F_n
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\delta_{\vZ_i}
&&\text{equal masses: proposal approximation}\\
\widehat F_{n,w}
&=\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\widetilde w(\vZ_i)\,\delta_{\vZ_i}}
        {\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\widetilde w(\vZ_i)}
&&\text{normalized weights: target approximation}
\end{align*}

Require $\sum_i\widetilde w(\vZ_i)>0$ and define
$$
g_n(\vz)=\frac{f(\vz)\widetilde w(\vz)}
{n^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\widetilde w(\vZ_j)}
$$

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{SN},n}
=\int f(\vx)\,\dif\widehat F_{n,w}(\vx)
=\int g_n(\vz)\,\dif\widehat F_n(\vz)
\quad\text{(generally biased)}
\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mu
$$

::: {.key-point}
[Weight the empirical distribution]{.alert} or [weight the function]{.alert}: the same estimate
:::

::: {.notes}
Motivation: an ordinary empirical distribution of the IID proposals
approximates the proposal law, whereas we want target expectations and
probabilities. Importance weighting changes the probability mass assigned
to each observed point to account for the target/proposal density ratio.
Normalizing those masses gives a discrete probability distribution that
can be reused for different functions without changing the sampled points.
For f equal to an indicator of a set A, the displayed integral estimates
the target probability of A; other choices estimate target means or moments.
This is not a construction specifically for repeated data: distinct points
can receive unequal masses. For weights 1, 2, 7 the masses are 0.1, 0.2, 0.7.
At finite n, the weighted empirical distribution generally differs from
the target distribution.

Recall [Markov Chain Monte Carlo: empirical distributions]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#empirical-distributions).
Use the same $\widehat F_n$ and point-mass $\delta_{\vx_i}$ notation as the
empirical-distribution development in Markov Chain Monte Carlo, with the
subscript $w$ recording the weights. The points still have the proposal law;
weighting changes their empirical masses, not their locations or sampling law.
The estimator converges almost surely to mu under the support and integrability assumptions stated
on the self-normalization slides. The weights need only be proportional to
the normalized density ratio.
The denominator can be zero at finite $n$ if every sampled weight is zero.

The displayed equality is exact for each sample with positive total weight.
The function g_n depends on the whole sample through its denominator; it is
not the fixed ordinary-IS contribution g=f w. Both Fhat_n and Fhat_n,w
on this slide are probability distributions. Without self-normalization,
ordinary IS assigns masses w(Z_i)/n, whose total generally differs from one.
Ordinary importance sampling is unbiased for integrable $f$; self-normalization
produces a probability measure but generally loses finite-sample unbiasedness.
The weighted-distribution view also connects integration error to discrepancy:
the error is the integral of f against Fhat_n,w minus F_tar. Under the
appropriate RKHS assumptions, its absolute value is bounded by the RKHS
norm of f times the kernel discrepancy between these two distributions.
This bound uses fixed f; applying a bound to the sample-dependent g_n
requires care and is not a fixed-integrand argument.
Full support coverage is needed to approximate the whole target distribution,
which is stronger than covering only the support of $f\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$
for one particular integral. A weighted empirical approximation to the target
also does not imply that the scalar importance contribution $f(\vZ)w(\vZ)$
has the same distribution as $f(\vX)$.
:::

---

### Weighted samples and discrepancy {#weighted-samples-and-discrepancy}

The [same discrepancy principle]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#worst-case-integration-error) applies to normalized weighted samples

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{SN},n}-\mu
=\int f(\vx)\,\dif\bigl(\widehat F_{n,w}-F_{\mathrm{tar}}\bigr)(\vx)
$$

For $f\in\mathcal H_K$ with bounded target integration, define

$$
D\bigl(F_{\mathrm{tar}},\widehat F_{n,w};K\bigr)
=\sup_{\norm{h}_{\mathcal H_K}\le1}
\left|\int h\,\dif\bigl(\widehat F_{n,w}-F_{\mathrm{tar}}\bigr)\right|
$$

$$
\abs{\hmu_{\mathrm{SN},n}-\mu}
\le D\bigl(F_{\mathrm{tar}},\widehat F_{n,w};K\bigr)
\operatorname{vtn}_K(f)
$$

- Generally $\operatorname{vtn}_K(f)=\norm{f}_{\mathcal H_K}$
- If $1\in\mathcal H_K$, use $\operatorname{vtn}_K(f)=\min_{c\in\reals}\norm{f-c}_{\mathcal H_K}$ since the masses sum to one

::: {.key-point}
Compare [weighted samples with the target]{.alert}; separate discrepancy from function variation
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a deterministic inequality for every realized sample with positive
total weight. It does not require unbiasedness or independence of the
normalized weights, and it is not by itself a confidence interval.
The source draws remain IID under the preceding construction; the normalized
weights depend on the whole sample.

Assume a measurable positive definite kernel with finite diagonal at every
sample point and bounded integration against the normalized target on H_K.
The earlier sufficient condition integral sqrt(K(x,x)) dF_tar(x) < infinity
ensures bounded target integration. Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the RKHS
representer of the error gives the displayed bound and the usual kernel
discrepancy. The supremum uses h as a dummy function and is distinct from
the sample-dependent g_n on the preceding slide.

Both distributions have total mass one, so integrating f-c gives the same
error as integrating f. When constants belong to H_K, minimize the norm
over c to obtain the sharper variation. The same weighted distribution can
be assessed for many different fixed f in the RKHS.

This connection is an error characterization, not an automatic computable
error certificate. Computing the discrepancy generally requires target
kernel integrals, which may be unavailable when the target normalizer is
unknown. No convergence rate for this discrepancy is asserted here.
:::

---

### One importance ratio, three methods {#one-importance-ratio-three-methods}

For [ordinary IS]{.alert}, acceptance–rejection, and the independence sampler, use
$w=\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}/\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ with the same IID proposal law

| | [Ordinary IS](#importance-sampling) | [Acceptance–rejection]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#acceptancerejection-sampling) | [Metropolized<br>independence]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#the-independence-sampler) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Rule | Contribution $f(\vZ_i)w(\vZ_i)$ | Accept with probability $w(\vz)/M$ | Accept with probability $\min\{1,w(\vz)/w(\vx)\}$ |
| Rejection | None; keep every proposal | Discard; try again | Repeat current state |
| Output | IID weighted contributions | IID target draws | Chain states;<br>target invariant |
| Global envelope | None required | Known $M\ge\sup_{\vx}w(\vx)$ | None required |

::: {.key-point}
[Weight contributions]{.alert} · [select observations]{.alert} · [update a chain]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
The three columns target the same expectation but use the importance ratio
differently. Ordinary importance sampling averages all f(Z_i)w(Z_i), with the
normalized ratio available and f integrable under the target. The proposals
retain their proposal distribution; weighting does not turn them into target
draws. The independence-sampler column recalls the construction in Markov Chain
Monte Carlo; its states are generally dependent.

Acceptance–rejection needs a known global envelope. The displayed w uses
normalized target and proposal densities. As in Generating Samples, it is
enough to know an unnormalized target and a matching envelope: neither the
target normalizer nor a normalized importance ratio is required. Use fresh
independent proposals and decision uniforms, and continue until the required
number of acceptances; only accepted observations enter its target average.

Self-normalized IS uses all proposals too, but forms a ratio of averages
instead of the ordinary IS contribution average shown in this table. Its
finite-sample bias and consistency were developed separately above.

Metropolized independence requires ratios of importance weights, without a
global envelope. Record a state at every iteration, including repeats after
rejection. Longer residence in a high-weight state supplies representation
through repetition, whereas importance sampling uses explicit contribution
weights. The chain has the target as an invariant distribution; this does not
give exact target marginals from an arbitrary start or finite-sample unbiasedness
of its average. Bounded weights can help its mixing even though a known global
bound is not needed to implement it.

All columns here use IID proposal draws and proposal coverage of the entire
target support. For one importance-sampling integral, covering only the support
of f times the target density suffices. For the ideal proposal equal to the
target, w=1 and acceptance–rejection with M=1 and Metropolized independence
both accept every proposal. All three then give ordinary target Monte Carlo.
:::

## Choosing a transformation {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="analysis-importance"}

- Variable transformation and importance sampling are intertwined
- The sampling density changes the variance of the sample mean
- Require
  - a finite Jacobian determinant
  - a proposal density that does not vanish where the integrand is nonzero
- Pilot samples can guide the choice of transformation or proposal

::: {.key-point}
Place more samples where the [magnitude]{.alert} of the integrand times the target density is large, without creating [extreme]{.alert} weights
:::

## Cost of an accurate IID estimate {#cost-for-iid-accuracy .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-error"}

For an [unbiased IID sample mean]{.alert} of $Y_g=g(\vZ)$, write
$\Ex(Y_g)=\mu$ and $\sigma^2(g)=\var\{g(\vZ)\}$

- $\$(g)$: generate $\vZ_i$ and evaluate $g(\vZ_i)$ with all required transforms
- $S(g)$: setup and independent-pilot cost

\begin{align*}
\text{Time cost for }n\text{ samples}\qquad T(n;g)&=S(g)+n\$(g)\\
\varepsilon&=\operatorname{RMSE}(\hmu_{g,n})=\frac{\sigma(g)}{\sqrt n}\\
\varepsilon^2&=\frac{\sigma^2(g)}n
\implies n=\frac{\sigma^2(g)}{\varepsilon^2}\\
\text{Time cost for }\alerttext{RMSE } \varepsilon\qquad C(\varepsilon;g)&=T\!\left(\frac{\sigma^2(g)}{\varepsilon^2};g\right)
=S(g)+\frac{\sigma^2(g)\$(g)}{\varepsilon^2}
\end{align*}

- For simplicity, we may [omit]{.alert} $S(g)$
- Practical comparisons should compare $C(\varepsilon;g)$, not $T(n;g)$

::: {.notes}
This is a planning model for independent, identically distributed,
unbiased contributions with finite variance and a fixed sample count.
The sampling law is part of the notation sigma(g). Cost includes random-input
generation, transforms, weights, controls, and the final evaluation, not just
calling a payoff function. Use one consistent unit: seconds, operation counts,
or money. T denotes time when those units are seconds; C denotes cost at a
specified accuracy. Setup is charged once per final calculation.
Retain S(g) in the complete model for completeness, but exercises and simple
method comparisons may explicitly ignore setup and pilot cost. This is a
modeling simplification, not a claim that those costs vanish or are always
negligible. When actual runtimes are measured, charge the work performed.

For known variance and positive epsilon, the exact sample count in this model
is max{1, ceil(sigma^2(g)/epsilon^2)}; the displayed approximation ignores
integer rounding. The one-contribution minimum also covers zero variance.
Unknown variance requires estimation and an error-assessment procedure;
this formula alone is not a certified adaptive stopping rule. An RMSE target
is not a deterministic absolute-error guarantee. A nominal CLT confidence
radius z sigma(g)/sqrt(n) instead introduces z^2 into the leading cost.
:::

---

### Compare work at the same accuracy

Ignoring setup and integer rounding, an equal-mean alternative $g(\vZ)$
improves on $f(\vX)$ when

$$
\sigma^2(g)\$(g)<\sigma^2(f)\$(f)
$$

- Half the variance at twice the cost: the [same]{.alert} leading work
- Setup and pilot fitting can change the winner at a finite tolerance

More generally, compare

$$
S(g)+\frac{\sigma^2(g)\$(g)}{\varepsilon^2}
\quad\text{with}\quad
S(f)+\frac{\sigma^2(f)\$(f)}{\varepsilon^2}
$$

::: {.key-point}
For IID means, compare [variance $\times$ cost per contribution]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
For fixed representations, setup costs, and sampling laws, the leading
epsilon^{-2} rate is the same. Variance reduction changes the constant.
If a_g=sigma^2(g) cost(g) is smaller than a_f but S(g)>S(f),
the approximation favors g only when
epsilon^2 < (a_f-a_g)/(S(g)-S(f)). This explains why an expensive pilot may
pay off for a tight tolerance but not for a loose one. If a representation
or pilot size is retuned as epsilon changes, retain that dependence rather
than treating S(g) and a_g as constants.
Exact transport preserves the output variance but can change sampling cost;
importance sampling can change both factors. Later, apply this same
comparison to a controlled or conditional contribution. These are costs for
estimating a mean, not for producing a target-distributed sample.
:::

# Control Variates and Conditioning {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-reduction"}

- [Control variates](#control-variates)
- [Conditional Monte Carlo](#conditional-monte-carlo)
- [Conditioning an Asian average](#conditioning-an-asian-average)

## Control variates {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-reduction"}

Let $\boldsymbol{\eta}(\vX)=(\eta_1(\vX),\ldots,\eta_m(\vX))^\mathsf T$
have known [zero]{.alert} mean

For fixed coefficients $\vbeta$, define

$$
Y_{\mathrm{CV}}=g_{\mathrm{CV}}(\vX)=f(\vX)-\vbeta^\mathsf T\boldsymbol{\eta}(\vX)
$$

Then $\Ex(Y_{\mathrm{CV}})=\Ex[f(\vX)]=\mu$, so

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{CV},n}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}Y_{\mathrm{CV},i}
$$

is unbiased

::: {.key-point}
Choose $\vbeta$ to make $\var(Y_{\mathrm{CV}})$ as [small]{.alert} as possible
:::

---

### Optimal coefficients from covariances

$Y=f(\vX)$, $\boldsymbol{\eta}=\boldsymbol{\eta}(\vX)$, $\Ex(\boldsymbol{\eta})=\vzero$

Define the control covariance matrix and response–control covariances:

\begin{align*}
\mSigma_\eta&=\cov(\boldsymbol{\eta},\boldsymbol{\eta}),&
(\mSigma_\eta)_{jk}&=\cov(\eta_j,\eta_k),\\
\boldsymbol{\kappa}&=\cov(\boldsymbol{\eta},Y),&
\kappa_j&=\cov\{\eta_j(\vX),f(\vX)\}
\end{align*}

Since $Y_{\mathrm{CV}}-\mu=(Y-\mu)-\vbeta^\mathsf T\boldsymbol{\eta}$,

\begin{align*}
\var(Y_{\mathrm{CV}})
&=\Ex\bigl[((Y-\mu)-\vbeta^\mathsf T\boldsymbol{\eta})^2\bigr]\\
&=\var(Y)-2\vbeta^\mathsf T\boldsymbol{\kappa}
  +\vbeta^\mathsf T\mSigma_\eta\vbeta
\end{align*}

The variance is a [quadratic]{.alert} function of the coefficients

---

### Minimize the control-variate variance

For [nonsingular]{.alert} $\mSigma_\eta$, differentiate and set the gradient to zero:

\begin{align*}
\nabla_{\vbeta}\var(Y_{\mathrm{CV}})
&=-2\boldsymbol{\kappa}+2\mSigma_\eta\vbeta=\vzero,\\
\mSigma_\eta\vbeta_*&=\boldsymbol{\kappa},\qquad
\vbeta_*=\mSigma_\eta^{-1}\boldsymbol{\kappa}
\end{align*}

Completing the square confirms the minimum:

\begin{align*}
\var(Y_{\mathrm{CV}})
&=\var(Y)-\boldsymbol{\kappa}^\mathsf T\mSigma_\eta^{-1}\boldsymbol{\kappa}\\
&\quad +(\vbeta-\vbeta_*)^\mathsf T\mSigma_\eta(\vbeta-\vbeta_*)
\end{align*}

- Minimum variance: $\var(Y)-\boldsymbol{\kappa}^\mathsf T\mSigma_\eta^{-1}\boldsymbol{\kappa}$
- One control: $\beta_*=\cov\{f(\vX),\eta_1(\vX)\}/\var\{\eta_1(\vX)\}$

::: {.notes}
Assume finite second moments. A nonsingular covariance matrix is positive
definite, so the final quadratic term is nonnegative and the minimizer is
unique. With redundant controls, the covariance matrix can be singular;
remove redundant controls or solve the normal equations with a pseudoinverse.
The cross-covariance vector is in the covariance matrix's range, and the
optimal residual is unchanged by coefficient directions in its null space.
At the optimum, cov(eta, Y_CV)=kappa-Sigma_eta beta_*=0: the residual is
uncorrelated with every control. In practice, solve the covariance system
rather than explicitly forming the inverse.
:::

---

### One control: variance and cost

Suppose $\Ex(\eta)=0$ and

$$
\var(Y)=9,\qquad \var(\eta)=4,\qquad \cov(Y,\eta)=3
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Use $Y_{\mathrm{CV}}=Y-\beta\eta$
<span class="exsub">Find $\beta_*$ and the minimum contribution variance</span>
<span class="exsub">If a controlled contribution costs twice as much, which method needs less work for the same IID RMSE?</span>
<span class="exsub">Why fit $\beta$ on an independent pilot?</span>
</span>
:::

Use $\sigma^2(g_{\mathrm{CV}})\$(g_{\mathrm{CV}})$ versus $\sigma^2(f)\$(f)$; ignore setup and pilot cost

::: {.notes}
The optimal coefficient is 3/4, and the minimum variance is
9-3^2/4=27/4=6.75. If a direct contribution costs c, compare 9c
with (27/4)(2c)=13.5c. The direct method needs less work for the same
IID RMSE, ignoring setup, pilot costs, and integer sample counts.
An independent pilot makes the fitted coefficient independent of the
main samples. Conditional on the pilot, the control still has mean zero,
so the final mean remains unbiased, assuming integrability. Fitting on
the main samples does not generally retain exact unbiasedness.
Use the earlier cost model with g_CV(x)=f(x)-beta eta(x), so cost(g_CV)
charges for the whole controlled contribution. For one optimal control with
correlation rho, sigma^2(g_CV)=sigma^2(f)(1-rho^2). Ignoring setup,
CV saves work exactly when (1-rho^2) cost(g_CV)<cost(f).
If cost(g_CV)=2 cost(f), this requires rho^2>1/2; here rho^2=1/4.
For coefficients fitted on an independent pilot, the conditional IID formula
uses the realized residual variance. Unconditionally, average that variance
over the pilot, assuming the required finite moments, and charge the pilot.
:::

---

### Choosing coefficients by least squares

[Center]{.alert} the response and control values:

\begin{align*}
y_i&=f(\vx_i),& c_i&=y_i-\overline y,\\
H_{ij}&=\eta_j(\vx_i)-\overline{\eta}_j
\end{align*}

Then

$$
\hvbeta=\argmin_{\vb}\norm{\vc-\mH\vb}^2
$$

When $\mH^\mathsf T\mH$ is nonsingular,

$$
\hvbeta=(\mH^\mathsf T\mH)^{-1}\mH^\mathsf T\vc
$$

Sample covariances: $\widehat{\mSigma}_\eta=\mH^\mathsf T\mH/(n-1)$, $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}=\mH^\mathsf T\vc/(n-1)$

The residual is [orthogonal]{.alert} to the column space of $\mH$

::: {.notes}
Use an independent pilot to estimate beta
if exact unbiasedness of the final IID estimator is required.
:::

---

### Practical control-variate choices

- Good controls are [inexpensive]{.alert}, have known means, and are [strongly related]{.alert} to $f$
- More controls can reduce the sample size needed for a target accuracy
- Poor controls may increase computation without reducing variance
- For IID sampling, least squares targets variance reduction
- For low discrepancy sampling, choose coefficients to reduce [variation]{.alert}, not sampling variance

::: {.key-point}
A control variate turns [known]{.alert} expectations into information about an unknown expectation
:::

## Conditional Monte Carlo {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-probability"}

Let $V$ be a conditioning variable<br>
Recall the [laws of total expectation and variance]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#laws-of-total-expectation-and-variance)

\begin{align*}
\Ex(Y)&=\Ex_V\{\Ex(Y\mid V)\},\\
\var(Y)&=\Ex_V\{\var(Y\mid V)\}+\var_V\{\Ex(Y\mid V)\}
\end{align*}

Therefore

$$
\var_V\{\Ex(Y\mid V)\}\le\var(Y)
$$

If $Y=f(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ and

$$
Y_{\mathrm{CMC}}=g_{\mathrm{CMC}}(\vX_{2:d})=\Ex(Y\mid \vX_{2:d})
$$

is analytic, estimate $\mu$ by averaging $Y_{\mathrm{CMC},i}$ instead of $Y_i$

[Analytically averaging]{.alert} over part of the randomness [reduces]{.alert} variance

---

### Conditional density estimation

Write the simulator on uniform inputs as $Y=h(\vU)$ with $\vU\sim\Unif[0,1]^d$

Suppose $h$ is [increasing]{.alert} in $u_1$ and

$$
y=h(u_1,\vu_{2:d})\iff u_1=g(y;\vu_{2:d})
$$

Extend the inverse by clipping to $[0,1]$ outside the conditional support<br>
Then

\begin{align*}
F_{Y\mid \vU_{2:d}}(y\mid \vu_{2:d})
&=\Prob\{U_1\le g(y;\vu_{2:d})\}\\
&=g(y;\vu_{2:d}),\\
\varrho_Y(y)
&=\int_{[0,1]^{d-1}}\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}(y;\vu_{2:d})\,\dif\vu_{2:d}
\end{align*}

Thus a density value becomes an [expectation]{.alert} of a conditional density

---

### Density of a sum of uniforms

Let

$$
Y=\gamma_1U_1+\cdots+\gamma_dU_d,
\qquad \vU\sim\Unif[0,1]^d,
\qquad \gamma_j>0
$$

Solving for $u_1$ gives

$$
g(y;\vu_{2:d})=\frac{y-\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_ju_j}{\gamma_1}
$$

when $\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_ju_j\le y\le\gamma_1+\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_ju_j$

Hence

$$
\varrho_Y(y)=\Ex\!\left[
\frac1{\gamma_1}\indic\!\left\{
\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jU_j\le y\le
\gamma_1+\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jU_j
\right\}\right]
$$

[Conditional Monte Carlo notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/sampling/ConditionalMonteCarlo.ipynb)


---

### Condition a sum of two uniforms

Let $U_1,U_2\ \IIDsim\Unif(0,1)$ and $Y=U_1+U_2$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Condition on $U_2=v$
<span class="exsub">Find $F_{Y\mid U_2}(y\mid v)$ and $\varrho_{Y\mid U_2}(y\mid v)$</span>
<span class="exsub">Average over $v$ to obtain the triangular density of $Y$</span>
<span class="exsub">Why is the sample average of these conditional densities unbiased at each fixed $y$?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The conditional CDF is min(1,max(0,y-v)); a conditional-density version
is the indicator of v<y<v+1. Averaging over v in (0,1) gives y for
0<y<=1, 2-y for 1<y<2, and zero outside (0,2), with endpoint values
chosen consistently. For independent uniform conditioning draws V_i,
the sample average of the indicators has expectation equal to this
density by the law of total expectation. This estimates a density value;
it does not construct a new sample of Y. Avoid differentiating at the
conditional CDF's corners; density versions can differ on null sets.
:::

---

### Histograms, KDE, and conditional density

Output samples $Y_i$, equal-width bins $I_k$ of width $b$, kernel $\kappa$ with $\int\kappa=1$

\begin{align*}
\widehat\varrho_{\mathrm{Hist}}(y)
&=\frac1{nb}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\indic\{Y_i\in I_k\},\quad y\in I_k\\
\widehat\varrho_{\mathrm{KDE}}(y)
&=\frac1{nb}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\kappa\!\left(\frac{y-Y_i}{b}\right)\\
\widehat\varrho_{\mathrm{CMC}}(y)
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\varrho_{Y\mid V}(y\mid V_i)
\end{align*}

- Histogram and KDE: choose [bin width or bandwidth]{.alert}; finite-width smoothing generally introduces bias
- CMC: average the [analytic]{.alert} conditional density; no smoothing bandwidth
- Density error still depends on conditioning, sample design, and work

[Notebook: curves and repeated-run errors](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/sampling/ConditionalMonteCarlo.ipynb)

## Conditioning an Asian average {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="quant-finance"}

Equally spaced dates $t_j=j\Delta t$, $\Delta t=T/d$, arithmetic average $A$

\begin{align*}
S(t_j)&=S_0\exp\{(r-\sigma^2/2)t_j+\sigma B(t_j)\}\\
A&=\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^d S(t_j)
\end{align*}

[Integrate out]{.alert} the first Brownian increment

$$
B(t_j)=\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_1+R_j,\qquad Z_1\sim\Norm(0,1),\qquad R_1=0
$$

$Z_1$ independent of $\vR=(R_2,\ldots,R_d)$, formed from the remaining increments

\begin{align*}
C(\vR)&=\frac{S_0}{d}\sum_{j=1}^d
\exp\{(r-\sigma^2/2)t_j+\sigma R_j\}\\
A&=C(\vR)\exp(sZ_1),\qquad s=\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}>0
\end{align*}

---

### Conditional density of an Asian average

Given $C$, the average $A=C\exp(sZ_1)$ is [lognormal]{.alert}<br>
$\phi$ and $\Phi$: standard normal density and CDF

For $a>0$,

\begin{align*}
F_{A\mid C}(a\mid C)&=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\log(a/C)}s\right)\\
\varrho_{A\mid C}(a\mid C)&=\frac1{as}\phi\!\left(\frac{\log(a/C)}s\right)\\
\varrho_A(a)&=\Ex\!\left[\frac1{as}\phi\!\left(\frac{\log(a/C)}s\right)\right]
\end{align*}

- Sample the $d-1$ residual increments with IID or randomized low discrepancy points
- Average conditional densities; no exact arithmetic-Asian density needed
- Notebook: weekly $d=52$; compare CMC, histogram, and KDE at the selected $n$

---

### Asian-call payoff distribution

Discounted call payoff $P=e^{-rT}(A-K)_+$

\begin{align*}
\Prob(P=0)&=F_A(K)
=\Ex\!\left[\Phi\!\left(\frac{\log(K/C)}s\right)\right]\\
\varrho_P(p)&=e^{rT}\varrho_A(K+e^{rT}p),\qquad p>0\\
\int_0^\infty\varrho_P(p)\,\dif p&=1-F_A(K)
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
The [atom at zero]{.alert} and the density on positive payoffs are separate parts of the distribution
:::

Ordinary KDE on all payoffs blurs the zero-payoff atom into a smooth bump

[Notebook: average density, payoff density, and CMC option price](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/sampling/ConditionalMonteCarlo.ipynb)

---

### Combining efficiency methods {#combining-efficiency-methods}

::: {.key-point}
[Usually yes]{.alert}: combine compatible methods<br>
Their gains need [neither add nor multiply]{.alert}
:::

- One method changes the contribution seen by the next; benefits may [overlap]{.alert}
- Refit controls and reconsider the proposal after changing the contribution
- Apply antithetic, stratified, or low discrepancy inputs to the resulting cube integrand
- Compare the [combined]{.alert} method at equal computational work using independent replications

[Asian-option notebook: plain, drift, control, and both](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/performance/AsianOptionVarianceReduction.ipynb#Compare-independent-replications)<br>
Repeat the comparison with IID and randomized low discrepancy inputs

::: {.notes}
This is a bridge from changing contributions to changing sampling designs.
Students need not wait until the end of the deck for an answer to whether the
methods can be combined. The Asian-option companion already combines
importance sampling and control variates with IID or randomized low
discrepancy inputs, and repeats the comparisons for the lookback payoff.

There is no general rule that the separate reductions in variance add, or
that their reduction factors multiply. Each method acts on the contribution
remaining after the previous changes. For example, importance sampling alters
the covariance with a control, and conditioning can remove variation that a
control was already explaining. Refit controls for the resulting contribution;
under importance sampling, weight the control consistently and retain its
correct known mean. Conditional expectations must use the appropriate law.
Antithetic maps must preserve the sampling law to which they are applied.

For finite-variance contributions, exact conditioning cannot increase IID
variance relative to the contribution being conditioned. Optimally chosen
population control coefficients cannot increase IID variance because zero
coefficients remain available. These guarantees do not make the separate
gains additive or multiplicative, and do not guarantee lower computational
cost. Estimated coefficients, an unsuitable importance proposal, or a
sampling design that interacts poorly with the new integrand may give less
benefit or worse performance. Low discrepancy performance depends on the
resulting cube integrand and cannot be inferred from IID variance alone.
Assess the final estimator, include pilot and transformation work, and use
independent replications rather than within-design IID error formulas for
dependent inputs.
:::

## Antithetic sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-probability"}

If $\vA(\vX)$ has the same distribution as $\vX$, pair $f(\vX_i)$ with
$f\bigl(\vA(\vX_i)\bigr)$:

$$
Y_{\mathrm{Anti}}=\{f(\vX)+f(\vA(\vX))\}/2
$$

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{Anti},n}=\frac1m\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}Y_{\mathrm{Anti},i},\qquad n=2m\text{ evaluations}
$$

Examples (uniform-input pairing uses the composed integrand $h$):

\begin{align*}
\vA(\vU)&=\vone-\vU,& \vU&\sim\Unif[0,1]^d,\\
\vA(\vX)&=-\vX,& \vX&\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mSigma)
\end{align*}

[Dependent]{.alert} values within each pair; [independent]{.alert} pairs across $i$

The variance is

$$
\var(\hmu_{\mathrm{Anti},n})
=\frac{\var\{f(\vX)\}}{n}
\left[1+\corr\{f(\vX),f(\vA(\vX))\}\right]
$$

Antithetic sampling helps with [negatively]{.alert} correlated pairs · [Notebook comparison](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/performance/AsianOptionVarianceReduction.ipynb#Antithetic-pairs-at-equal-payoff-cost)

## Constructing an antithetic variate {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

If $X$ has continuous CDF $F$, then

\begin{gather*}
U=F(X)\sim\Unif[0,1],\\
1-U\sim\Unif[0,1],\\
A(X)=F^{-1}\bigl(1-F(X)\bigr)\sim F
\end{gather*}

For a symmetric distribution, this often reduces to reflection about the center

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>For which monotone functions $f$ does $f(X)$ become negatively correlated
with $f\bigl(A(X)\bigr)$?</span>
:::

## IID variance comparison

$Y=f(\vX)$, $\vX\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$, $\vZ\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$;
$w=\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}/\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$

Use $n$ independent contributions, or $n/2$ independent antithetic pairs

| Method | Contribution | Estimator variance |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Direct IID | $Y=f(\vX)$ | $\var(Y)/n$ |
| Exact transport | $Y_T=f(\vT(\vZ))$ | $\var(Y)/n$ |
| Importance sampling | $Y_{\mathrm{IS}}=w(\vZ)f(\vZ)$ | $\var(Y_{\mathrm{IS}})/n$ |
| Control variate | $Y_{\mathrm{CV}}=Y-\vbeta^\mathsf T\boldsymbol{\eta}(\vX)$ | $\var(Y_{\mathrm{CV}})/n$ |
| Conditional Monte Carlo | $Y_{\mathrm{CMC}}=\Ex(Y\mid V)$ | $\var(Y_{\mathrm{CMC}})/n\le\var(Y)/n$ |
| Antithetic pairs | $Y_{\mathrm{Anti}}=\{Y+f(\vA(\vX))\}/2$ | $\var(Y)(1+\rho)/n$ |

[Equal sample counts]{.alert} need not mean equal computational [work]{.alert}

---

### Conditions behind the comparison

- Exact transport: $\vT(\vZ)\stackrel d=\vX$
- Importance sampling: proposal covers the required support
- Control: $\Ex[\boldsymbol{\eta}(\vX)]=\vzero$; $\vbeta$ fixed or from an independent pilot
- Conditioning: compute $\Ex(Y\mid V)$ analytically, then sample $V$
- Antithetic: even $n$, $\vA(\vX)\stackrel d=\vX$;
  $\rho=\corr\{Y,f(\vA(\vX))\}$

::: {.notes}
All formulas assume finite second moments and independent contributions or
independent antithetic pairs. The antithetic row uses n evaluations of f;
the other rows use n contributions, whose evaluation costs can differ.
Conditional Monte Carlo may reduce dimension and avoid evaluating the full
original function. Compare variance times cost per contribution when choosing
between methods. Exact transport preserves the distribution of f(X).
:::

---

### Beyond the IID variance formulas

- Maps, weights, controls, and conditional expectations have different costs
- Latin hypercubes and randomized low discrepancy points use dependent inputs
- For low discrepancy sampling, error depends on integrand variation and point structure
- Use independent replications to assess randomized designs

::: {.notes}
The IID formulas do not apply to within-design sample variance for LHS or
randomized low discrepancy sampling. Exact transport can be better than
weighted importance sampling for a particular f; it does not imply that every
change of variables preserves variance. The Keister example changes the
unit-cube integrand, including its Jacobian.
:::

## Latin hypercube sampling in one dimension {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-reduction"}

For the cube integrand $h$, place [one]{.alert} independent uniform point in each of $n$ equal strata:

$$
U_i=\frac{i+V_i}{n},
\qquad V_i\ \IIDsim\ \Unif[0,1],
\qquad i=0,\ldots,n-1
$$

Define $\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}=n^{-1}\sum_i h(U_i)$<br>
Then $U_i\sim\Unif[i/n,(i+1)/n]$ and

\begin{align*}
\Ex(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\Ex\{h(U_i)\}\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\int_{i/n}^{(i+1)/n}h(u)\,\dif u\\
&=\int_0^1h(u)\,\dif u
\end{align*}

The $U_i$ are independent but [not]{.alert} identically distributed

---

### One-dimensional LHS variance

Because the strata are independent,

$$
\var(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\var\{h(U_i)\}
$$

For differentiable $h$, the mean value and Taylor theorems imply

\begin{align*}
\var(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
&\le\frac{\norm{h'}_\infty^2}{n^3},\\
\operatorname{RMSE}(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
&\le\frac{\norm{h'}_\infty}{n^{3/2}}
\end{align*}

In one dimension, stratification can improve the IID $n^{-1/2}$ RMSE rate to $n^{-3/2}$ for smooth $h$

---

### Latin hypercube sampling in $d$ dimensions

Let $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_d$ be independent random permutations of $0,\ldots,n-1$:

$$
U_{i\ell}=\frac{\pi_\ell(i)+V_{i\ell}}n,
\qquad V_{i\ell}\ \IIDsim\ \Unif[0,1]
$$

Each point is $\vU_i=(U_{i1},\ldots,U_{id})$; each coordinate uses every stratum [exactly once]{.alert}

Random permutations make every $\vU_i$ marginally uniform; the points are dependent

For $R$ independent Latin hypercubes,

\begin{align*}
\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}^{(r)}
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}h(\vU_i^{(r)}),\\
\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n,R}
&=\frac1R\sum_{r=1}^R\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}^{(r)},\\
\widehat{\var}(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n,R})
&=\frac1{R(R-1)}\sum_{r=1}^R
\left(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}^{(r)}-\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n,R}\right)^2
\end{align*}

## Comparing random designs {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-low-discrepancy"}

Each design has $n=64$ points in $[0,1]^2$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "IID, Latin hypercube, and scrambled Sobol' point sets with 64 points in the unit square"
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 96%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import qmc

plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "stix"
n = 64
rng = np.random.default_rng(56504)
designs = {
    "IID": rng.random((n, 2)),
    "Latin hypercube": qmc.LatinHypercube(d=2, seed=56504).random(n),
    "Scrambled Sobol'": qmc.Sobol(d=2, scramble=True, seed=56504).random_base2(6),
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 4.2), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, (title, points) in zip(axes, designs.items()):
    ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], s=24, color="#1f5a91", alpha=0.9)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=17)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$u_1$", fontsize=18, math_fontfamily="stix")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$u_2$", fontsize=18, math_fontfamily="stix")
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=11)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.14)
plt.show()
```

---

### Strengths and limitations of LHS

### Strengths

- [No]{.alert} importance density, control variate, or conditional expectation required
- Can converge [faster]{.alert} than IID sampling
- Guarantees one point in every one-dimensional [stratum]{.alert}

### Limitations

- The sample size is [fixed]{.alert} when the design is constructed
- Accuracy assessment requires [independent]{.alert} replications
- Too many replications can [erase]{.alert} the efficiency gain
- The one-dimensional $n^{-3/2}$ RMSE guarantee does [not]{.alert} extend automatically to $d>1$

## The van der Corput sequence {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy-sampling"}

Write a nonnegative integer in base $b$:

$$
i=(\cdots i_2i_1i_0)_b
$$

[Reverse]{.alert} the digits across the radix point:

$$
\phi_b(i)=(0.i_0i_1i_2\cdots)_b
=\frac{i_0}b+\frac{i_1}{b^2}+\frac{i_2}{b^3}+\cdots
$$

- Usually $b$ is prime; $b=2$ is common
- $\{\phi_b(i)\}_{i=0}^{b^m-1}$ contains the same points as $\{i/b^m\}_{i=0}^{b^m-1}$ in a different order
- Earlier points keep their order as the sample grows

::: {.key-point}
The van der Corput construction turns a fixed-size grid into an [extensible]{.alert} sequence
:::

---

### First points in base two

For $i=0,1,2,3$, reversing the binary digits gives

$$
\bigl(\phi_2(0),\phi_2(1),\phi_2(2),\phi_2(3)\bigr)
=\bigl(0,\frac12,\frac14,\frac34\bigr)
$$

The first four points form the grid $\{0,1/4,1/2,3/4\}$ in a different order

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Compute $\phi_2(4)$ and $\phi_2(5)$ and identify the two new eighths</span>
:::

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Compute $\phi_2(9)$, $\phi_2(14)$, and $\phi_2(19)$ by [reversing]{.alert} their binary digits</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The new values are $1/8$ and $5/8$, respectively: reverse the three binary
digits in $4=100_2$ and $5=101_2$ across the radix point.
For the larger indices, $9=1001_2$, $14=1110_2$, and $19=10011_2$ give
$\phi_2(9)=9/16$, $\phi_2(14)=7/16$, and $\phi_2(19)=25/32$.
:::

## Four low discrepancy families {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy-sampling"}

For $i=0,1,\ldots$:

| Family | Construction | Typical preferred size |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Kronecker | $\vu_i=i\vzeta\bmod1$ | none |
| Lattice | $\vu_i=\phi_b(i)\vzeta\bmod1$ | $n=b^m$ |
| Halton | $\vu_i=(\phi_2(i),\phi_3(i),\phi_5(i),\ldots)$ | none |
| Digital | $\vu_i=i_0\vc_0\oplus i_1\vc_1\oplus\cdots$ | $n=b^m$ |

Here $\oplus$ denotes digitwise addition modulo $b$

For basic Halton, choosing the coordinate bases fixes the sequence

Different families balance [extensibility]{.alert}, projection [quality]{.alert}, and [fast]{.alert} construction

[Low Discrepancy Constructions notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/sampling/LowDiscrepancyConstructions.ipynb): recover generators from the first points

### Lattice sequence: eight points

For the lattice sequence with $b=2$, generator $\vzeta=(1,3)$, and $n=8$,

$$
\vu_i=\phi_2(i)\vzeta\bmod1
$$

| $i$ | $(i)_2$ | $\phi_2(i)$ | $\zeta_1\phi_2(i)\bmod1=u_{i,1}$ | $\zeta_2\phi_2(i)\bmod1=u_{i,2}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | 000 | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| 1 | 001 | $1/2$ | $1/2$ | $1/2$ |
| 2 | 010 | $1/4$ | $1/4$ | $3/4$ |
| 3 | 011 | $3/4$ | $3/4$ | $1/4$ |
| 4 | 100 | $1/8$ | $1/8$ | $3/8$ |
| 5 | 101 | $5/8$ | $5/8$ | $7/8$ |
| 6 | 110 | $3/8$ | $3/8$ | $1/8$ |
| 7 | 111 | $7/8$ | $7/8$ | $5/8$ |

For example, $i=5$ gives $\phi_2(5)=5/8$ and $3(5/8)=15/8\equiv7/8\pmod1$

### Kronecker sequence: four points

For hand arithmetic, take $\vzeta=(0.41,0.73)$ and $\vu_i=i\vzeta\bmod1$

| $i$ | $i\zeta_1\bmod1$ | $i\zeta_2\bmod1$ | $\vu_i$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | $0$ | $0$ | $(0,0)$ |
| 1 | $0.41$ | $0.73$ | $(0.41,0.73)$ |
| 2 | $0.82$ | $1.46\bmod1=0.46$ | $(0.82,0.46)$ |
| 3 | $1.23\bmod1=0.23$ | $2.19\bmod1=0.19$ | $(0.23,0.19)$ |

The decimal generator keeps this finite example easy to calculate by hand

In base two, let $i=i_0+2i_1$ and choose
$\vc_0=(1/2,1/2)$, $\vc_1=(1/4,3/4)$

| $i$ | $(i)_2$ | Generators used | $\vu_i=i_0\vc_0\oplus i_1\vc_1$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | 00 | none | $(0,0)$ |
| 1 | 01 | $\vc_0$ | $(1/2,1/2)$ |
