## Component-by-component construction {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

Generators for lattice rules and digital nets may be chosen by number theory or computer search

The component-by-component strategy:

1. Choose a one-dimensional generator that minimizes a discrepancy criterion over relevant sample sizes
2. Freeze the first $\ell$ components
3. Search for component $\ell+1$ that minimizes discrepancy
4. Increase $\ell$ and repeat until $\ell=d$

::: {.key-point}
A high-dimensional design is built by optimizing [one coordinate]{.alert} at a time
:::

## Randomized low discrepancy sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy-sampling"}

<span id="why-randomize"></span>

Randomization aims for

$$
\vU_{\mathrm{rand},i}\sim\Unif[0,1]^d
$$

for every $i$, while preserving low discrepancy jointly

- [Random shift]{.alert}: $\vU_{\mathrm{rand},i}=\vu_i+\vDelta\bmod1$, especially for lattices and Kronecker sequences
- [Random digital shift]{.alert}: $\vU_{\mathrm{rand},i}=\vu_i\oplus\vDelta$, especially for digital sequences
- Linear matrix or nested uniform [scrambling]{.alert}, especially for digital sequences

[Independent]{.alert} randomizations support error assessment without reverting to IID
point placement; recall the [earlier variance and RMSE comparison](#variance-reduction)

::: {.notes}
Each randomized point is marginally uniform, so its sample mean is unbiased.
Randomization almost surely avoids exact cube-boundary points, making Gaussian
quantile transforms finite. The opening variance slide states the nearly
$\Order(n^{-3/2})$ RMSE rate for sufficiently smooth integrands under nested
scrambling.
:::

---

### Shift the points you constructed

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>[Lattice:]{.alert} For your $\vzeta=(1,5)$ points, suppose the random shift is
$\vDelta=(1/4,1/2)$; find $(\vu_4+\vDelta)\bmod1$ and
$(\vu_5+\vDelta)\bmod1$</span>
:::

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>[Digital]{.alert}, $b=2$: For your points from $\vc_0,\vc_1,\vc_2$,
suppose the digital shift is $\vDelta=(3/8,1/4)$;
find $\vu_0\oplus\vDelta$ and $\vu_7\oplus\vDelta$</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Lattice: $\vu_4=(1/8,5/8)$ shifts to $(3/8,1/8)$, and
$\vu_5=(5/8,1/8)$ shifts to $(7/8,5/8)$.
Digital: $\vu_0=(0,0)$ shifts to $(3/8,1/4)$, and
$\vu_7=(7/8,5/8)$ shifts by binary digitwise addition to $(1/2,7/8)$.
The displayed shifts are particular realizations used for hand calculation;
the random shift is uniform on the unit square in the sampling method.
:::

---

### Variance of a randomized low discrepancy estimate {#rqmc-estimator-variance}

Recall $h(\vu)=g\bigl(\vS(\vu)\bigr)$, the complete calculation from [uniform inputs]{.alert}

Each $\vU_i\sim\Unif[0,1]^d$ but the points within a run are [dependent]{.alert}

\begin{align*}
\hmu_n(h)&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}h(\vU_i)
&\Ex_{\mathrm{rand}}\{\hmu_n(h)\}&=\mu\\
\operatorname{MSE}\{\hmu_n(h)\}
&=\var_{\mathrm{rand}}\{\hmu_n(h)\}\\
&=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}
\cov_{\mathrm{rand}}\{h(\vU_i),h(\vU_j)\}
\end{align*}

- IID points: off-diagonal covariances vanish
- Randomized LD: the [whole design]{.alert} determines the estimator variance

::: {.key-point}
For unbiased RQMC, RMSE is the SD of the [whole estimate]{.alert}

Estimate that SD using [independent runs under Stopping criteria](#stopping-criteria)
:::

::: {.notes}
Randomness here is in the points, with h fixed. It differs from the
Gaussian-process average-case interpretation in Markov Chain Monte Carlo,
where the points are fixed and the integrand is random. Marginal uniformity
and integrability give unbiasedness. Finite second moments justify the
covariance expansion. The diagonal terms sum to var{h(U)}/n, but RQMC
also has off-diagonal terms. Do not discard them or substitute within-run
sample variance divided by n as an RQMC variance estimate.
Independent shifts or scrambles provide independent complete-run estimates.
Their across-run sample variance estimates the variance of one whole run;
divide by the number of runs only when reporting the variance of their mean.
Source: [Owen (2026), Randomized quasi-Monte Carlo integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17143).
:::

## Stopping criteria {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="data-driven-error"}

For $\mu=\Ex[h(\vU)]$, assess integration error from computed values

::: {.key-point}
Every error assessment rests on [assumptions]{.alert}
:::

- Match the [sampling design]{.alert}: how the $\vu_i$ are generated and how they depend on one another
- Specify what is assumed about [the integrand $h$]{.alert}: moments, smoothness, coefficient decay, or a probabilistic model

The following routes use different combinations of these assumptions

- [IID recap](#iid-error-recap): normal-data and CLT intervals
- [IID guarantees with a kurtosis bound](#iid-berry-esseen): Berry–Esseen bounds
- [RQMC replications](#rqmc-error-replications): independent whole-design estimates
- [One fixed QMC design](#fixed-qmc-error-assessment): coefficient bounds or Bayesian intervals

::: {.notes}
The sampling design includes IID generation, dependence within a randomized
low discrepancy design, independence across replications, or a fixed point
set. Conditions on h are evaluated together with that design: for example,
normality and moments concern the induced outputs h(U), while smoothness or
coefficient decay concerns h itself. For Bayesian intervals, the probabilistic
integrand model supplies the interpretation of uncertainty. A method name
or returned error radius alone does not verify these assumptions.
:::

---

### IID recap {#iid-error-recap}

Let $s_n$ be the sample SD of the $n$ IID outputs $h(\vU_i)$

$$
\hmu_n\ \pm\ t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\,\frac{s_n}{\sqrt n}
$$

- [Normal IID outputs]{.alert}: exact $(1-\alpha)$ coverage at fixed $n$
- [CLT approximation]{.alert}: $n$ large enough for the [sample mean]{.alert} to be nearly normal<br>
  Also need $s_n$ to approximate the true SD well
- QMCPy: `CubMCCLT` uses a two-stage [CLT]{.alert} procedure with an inflated pilot SD

::: {.key-point}
Compare the interval radius with $\varepsilon$; justify [adaptive stopping]{.alert} separately
:::

::: {.notes}
The normality assumption concerns the scalar outputs h(U_i), not the uniform
inputs U_i. The Student-t confidence interval is exact for a fixed n with
independent identically distributed normal outputs and positive variance.
This is the interval obtained by inverting the two-sided t-test for the mean.
For general IID outputs with finite positive variance, a studentized CLT
justifies approximate coverage asymptotically. At a practical finite n, the
mean must be sufficiently close to normal and the sample SD sufficiently
representative of the true SD. A large n alone does not diagnose rare tails.
The normal critical value z_(1-alpha/2) is the CLT choice; the t critical value
is also asymptotically valid but is not an exact finite-sample correction for
nonnormal data. Neither fixed-n result automatically justifies repeatedly
checking and stopping when the displayed radius first falls below epsilon.
For RQMC, within-design values are dependent; replace the IID observations
by independent whole-design estimates. The later replication slides give
the formula and qualifications. CubMCCLT uses a normal quantile and an
inflated pilot SD, not the exact fixed-n normal-data Student-t procedure.
For that fixed-n interval, use scipy.stats.t.ppf(1-alpha/2, n-1) and the
ordinary sample SD (ddof=1); QMCPy has no separate IID Student-t stopping
class in this pinned version. An RMSE target and confidence coverage are
distinct error criteria. Budget exhausted does not mean tolerance met.
:::

---

### IID guarantees with a kurtosis bound {#iid-berry-esseen}

For $Y=h(\vU)$, assume a [known bound]{.alert} on ordinary kurtosis

$$
\kappa=\frac{\Ex[(Y-\mu)^4]}{\sigma^4}\le\kappa_{\max}
\qquad \sigma^2=\var(Y)>0
$$

- Berry–Esseen controls the normal-approximation error at finite sample size
- The kurtosis bound also controls the risk of underestimating SD from the pilot
- QMCPy: `CubMCG` combines a pilot with [Berry–Esseen/Chebyshev]{.alert} sample sizing
- Its admissible `kurtmax` comes from `n_init`, `inflate`, and `alpha`<br>
  Choose these so the assumed $\kappa_{\max}$ is within that admissible bound

::: {.key-point}
A sample kurtosis estimate does not establish a [known kurtosis bound]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
Kurtosis here is the standardized fourth central moment, not excess kurtosis;
a normal output has kappa=3. A bounded fourth moment controls the standardized
third absolute moment needed by Berry-Esseen and the variability of the pilot
variance estimator. This is a conditional guarantee for a specified class of
output distributions, not a universal guarantee from an apparently benign pilot.
In the pinned CubMCG, alpha_sigma=alpha/2 and
kurtmax=(n_init-3)/(n_init-1) + alpha_sigma*n_init/(1-alpha_sigma)
        * (1-1/inflate**2)**2.
There is no kurtmax constructor keyword. Increase n_init or adjust inflate
appropriately so this admissible cap covers the externally justified bound;
inspect sc.kurtmax after construction. The code uses inflate on the pilot SD.
An example call is sc=qmcpy.CubMCG(integrand, abs_tol=epsilon, rel_tol=0,
n_init=1024, inflate=1.2, alpha=0.01); these illustrative defaults are not a
claim that an arbitrary integrand satisfies the resulting kurtosis cap.
Call solution,data=sc.integrate(). Check the returned error bounds and budget
warnings; exhausting n_limit does not establish success. The same interface
applies to the other stopping classes, with class-specific parameters.
Source checked in the recorded qmcpy commit: stopping_criterion/cub_mc_g.py.
:::

---

### RQMC error assessment by independent replications {#rqmc-error-replications}

QMCPy: `CubQMCRepStudentT`

Independently randomize the [whole $n$-point design]{.alert} $R\ge2$ times

\begin{align*}
\hmu_n^{(r)}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}h(\vU_i^{(r)})
&&r=0,\ldots,R-1\\
\hmu_{R,n}&=\frac1R\sum_{r=0}^{R-1}\hmu_n^{(r)}
& \hat\sigma^2_{R,n}&=\frac1{R-1}\sum_{r=0}^{R-1}(\hmu_n^{(r)}-\hmu_{R,n})^2
\end{align*}

| Quantity | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| $\hat\sigma^2_{R,n}$ | Estimates $\sigma_n^2=\var_{\mathrm{rand}}\{\hmu_n(h)\}$ of one $n$-point run |
| $\hat\sigma^2_{R,n}/R$ | Estimates the variance of the reported mean $\hmu_{R,n}$ |

::: {.key-point}
Our $R$ observations are [independent sample averages]{.alert}, not individual function values
:::

::: {.notes}
Fix h, n, the design, and its randomization law across replications. The
$\hmu_n^{(r)}$ are IID and unbiased, with variance $\sigma_n^2$ when second
moments exist. Here $\hmu_{R,n}$ averages $R$ whole-run estimates, each based
on $n$ points, so the total point count is $Rn$. The observations used in
the sample-variance calculation are these R sample averages, not the
individual outputs h(U_i) within them. The latter are dependent within a run.
Then $\Ex[\hat\sigma^2_{R,n}]=\sigma_n^2$ and
$\var(\hmu_{R,n})=\sigma_n^2/R$ exactly at fixed $n$ and $R$.
The sample variance of the n function values within one randomized design
is not a substitute: it does not account for their covariances.
Each run uses an independent shift or scramble. Any fitted control must be
fixed in advance or have an appropriate independent-pilot analysis.
Source: [Owen (2026), Section 5.6](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.17143v1#S5.SS6).
:::

---

### A stopping criterion from replications {#rqmc-replication-stopping}

For a fixed $n$ and $R$, an approximate $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval is

$$
\hmu_{R,n}\ \pm\ t_{1-\alpha/2,R-1}\,\frac{\hat\sigma_{R,n}}{\sqrt R}
$$

$t_{1-\alpha/2,R-1}$ is a Student-$t$ quantile; $\alpha$ is the nominal failure probability

A candidate rule: increase $n$ and recompute until $t_{1-\alpha/2,R-1}\hat\sigma_{R,n}/\sqrt R\le\varepsilon$

- [Small $R$]{.alert} in `CubQMCRepStudentT`: assume the $\hmu_n^{(r)}$ are [nearly normal]{.alert}<br>
  This assumption is [not always known]{.alert} to hold
- [Adaptive stopping]{.alert}: repeated checks do not automatically preserve $1-\alpha$ coverage

::: {.key-point}
Even exact fixed-$n$ intervals need a [separate justification]{.alert} for data-dependent stopping
:::

::: {.notes}
This Student-t confidence interval is the interval counterpart of the
two-sided t-test for the mean of the independent replicate estimates. Keeping
R small relies on those whole-run estimates being close to normal; this
assumption may not be established for the chosen integrand and randomization.
At fixed n and R, this Student-t interval is exact for normal replicate
means; otherwise it is an approximation whose adequacy depends on their
distribution and R. Unbiasedness and finite variance alone do not make a
small-R t interval exact. Larger n does not universally make an individual
RQMC replicate asymptotically normal.
For nested designs, grow each run's n through admissible sizes, retaining
its randomization. Recompute the independent run means and their across-run
variance at the new n. A nominal fixed-sample interval does not automatically
retain its coverage at a data-dependent stopping time. This is a separate
issue from the normal/CLT approximation: even exact coverage at each fixed
n does not imply the same coverage at a data-dependent n. Merely changing
n on a predetermined schedule is not the problem; choosing when to report
an interval using the observed estimates or widths is.
Count all Rn function evaluations and the error-assessment work, including
any discarded pilot work. Increasing R until an interval is narrow enough
also requires a stopping-time coverage argument.
A justified sequential procedure can address this, for example by allocating
failure probabilities across a predetermined sequence of checks whose sum
is at most alpha, provided each check has the claimed valid marginal
coverage. Allocating alpha does not repair an unjustified t approximation.
Time-uniform intervals are another possibility under suitable assumptions;
ordinary fixed-sample t intervals do not automatically have that property.
The next two slides explain why the IID pilot strategy does not transfer
automatically and how points per design and replication count serve
different roles in accuracy and error assessment.
Sources: [Owen (2026), Section 5.6](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.17143v1#S5.SS6)
for replication intervals; [Howard et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08240)
for the distinction between fixed-sample and time-uniform coverage. The latter
is general sequential-inference guidance, not a ready-made confidence
sequence for arbitrary RQMC designs.
:::

---

### Why a small pilot does not determine RQMC error {#rqmc-pilot-sample-size}

\begin{align*}
\text{IID:}\quad\var\{\hmu_n(h)\}&=\frac{\sigma^2(h)}n
&\sigma^2(h)&=\var\{h(\vU)\}\\
\text{RQMC:}\quad\sigma_n^2&=\var_{\mathrm{rand}}\{\hmu_n(h)\}
\end{align*}

- IID: a pilot estimates $\sigma^2(h)$, which is [independent of $n$]{.alert}
- RQMC: $\hat\sigma^2_{R,n_0}$ estimates the variance of an [$n_0$-point run]{.alert}
- Changing $n$ changes the design and the covariances within each run

::: {.key-point}
A pilot at $n_0$ estimates $\sigma_{n_0}$; a large-$n$ interval needs $\sigma_n$

Extrapolation needs an additional, justified [scaling model]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
For IID contributions, an independent pilot estimates the same one-observation
variance used in the final sample-mean formula for any n. Its uncertainty
still matters, as in the earlier IID stopping discussion.
For RQMC, the across-run sample variance at n0 targets sigma_n0 squared,
not sigma_n squared for a larger design. There is no automatic IID scaling
sigma_n = sigma_n0 sqrt(n0/n): the off-diagonal covariances also change.
If an appropriate rate model and its validity range are known, extrapolation
may be possible, but a single small design does not establish that model.
To assess the new n directly, extend each independently randomized design
and recompute its mean before estimating the across-run variance.
:::

---

### Replication, efficiency, and interval justification {#rqmc-replication-efficiency}

| How the calculation grows | Accuracy and confidence intervals |
|:---|:---|
| Fix $n$, increase $R$ | Independent-run CLT as $R\to\infty$; RMSE decreases as $R^{-1/2}$ |
| Use large $n$ and modest $R$ | Exploit RQMC error decay; Student-$t$ intervals remain approximate |

For a fixed evaluation budget $N=Rn$,

$$
\operatorname{RMSE}\{\hmu_{R,n}\}
=\frac{\sigma_n}{\sqrt R}
\qquad
\sigma_n^2=\var_{\mathrm{rand}}\{\hmu_n(h)\}
$$

More replications leave [fewer points per design]{.alert}, changing $\sigma_n$

::: {.key-point}
Large $n$ supports [sample mean accuracy]{.alert}; large $R$ supports [confidence in error assessment]{.alert}

Choosing $n$ adaptively also needs a [stopping-time coverage argument]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
At fixed n, the independent run means have a fixed distribution. With finite
positive variance, increasing R supports the standard CLT and asymptotically
valid studentized intervals. This is not exact finite-R coverage in general.
For independent unbiased run estimates, RMSE equals sigma_n/sqrt(R)
exactly when the variance exists. At fixed total point count N, changing R
also changes n=N/R and therefore sigma_n. An accuracy comparison requires
information about how sigma_n changes with n; the later cost section
introduces a rate model for that purpose. No rate model is needed to explain
the interval-justification issue here.

The practical tension is strong replication-based CLT justification with
less efficient point allocation, versus efficient large RQMC designs with
approximate intervals from modest replication counts. Large n alone does
not provide a general normal limit for a fixed number of replications.
This describes the usual Student-t replication approach, not an impossibility
claim about all confidence procedures. Adaptive stopping needs the additional
coverage qualifications already stated.
Source: [Owen (2026), Section 5.6](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.17143v1#S5.SS6).
:::

---

### Error assessment for one fixed QMC design {#fixed-qmc-error-assessment}

For a [deterministic]{.alert} design, assess the integration error of the fixed $h$

Unknown $\operatorname{vtn}_K(h)$ prevents direct use of discrepancy $\times$ variation

| Error assessment | QMCPy class |
|:---|:---|
| Fourier coefficient bound | `CubQMCLatticeG` |
| Walsh coefficient bound | `CubQMCNetG` |
| Bayesian interval, lattice | `CubQMCBayesLatticeG` |
| Bayesian interval, digital net | `CubQMCBayesNetG` |

Coefficient bounds need decay assumptions; Bayesian intervals need an integrand model<br>
These classes exploit [matching sequences]{.alert} for fast calculations

::: {.key-point}
A fixed design has no replication variance<br>
Its error assessment needs [function-class assumptions]{.alert} or an [integrand model]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
For deterministic QMC, the discrepancy bound involves vtn_K(h), which is
also generally unknown. Fourier/Walsh coefficient-decay methods can give
computable bounds under stated function-class assumptions. A Bayesian
credible interval instead uses an integrand model.
The two groups distinguish available error-assessment routes, not mutually
exclusive algorithm families. A coefficient bound can also be applied to a
realized randomized design when its assumptions hold; independent replication
is the additional route supplied by randomization. One fixed deterministic
sequence has no randomization variance to estimate by replication. The sample
variance of its individual function values does not certify integration error.
Hickernell and collaborators' data-driven Fourier/Walsh bounds exploit
coefficient-decay assumptions rather than requiring the full variation as
an input. Function-class assumptions justify the bounds; matching lattice
or digital sequences also allow fast Fourier or Walsh coefficient calculations.
Refer to the later stopping notebooks for concrete implementations.
Bayesian credible intervals can use a fixed design by putting uncertainty
on h; their coverage is under that model, not a randomization guarantee for
an arbitrary fixed integrand. This matches the earlier average-case discussion.
Generic kernel calculations can be expensive. Certain kernels paired with
matching sequences give structured calculations and fast transforms, making
Bayesian error assessment fast as well. Computational speed and the model
assumptions supporting a credible interval are separate considerations.
For IID sampling, the familiar sample variance of individual h(U_i) values
divided by n estimates the variance of their mean; that calculation cannot
be transferred to dependent points within an RQMC run.
An RMSE target controls root mean squared error over randomizations; a
confidence interval also specifies a coverage level.
The target is the integral of the fixed cube integrand h. Use fixed points
u_i for deterministic QMC and randomized points U_i for RQMC. The generic
estimate notation is shared, but only the latter has randomization variance.
A stopping procedure must
supply a computable bound or interval and state the assumptions supporting it.
A theoretical variation bound may be unavailable; coefficient-decay methods
replace it with data-driven bounds for a specified function class.
Confidence and credible intervals have different interpretations. Neither
should be identified with an RMSE bound or an unconditional absolute-error
guarantee. The preceding IID and RQMC slides explain sampling-based
standard errors; the next slides compare concrete stopping implementations.
:::

### Stopping rules in action

- [Keister notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/applications/KeisterExample.ipynb#Practical-stopping-criteria): IID CLT, independent Sobol' replications, and a Walsh-coefficient bound
- [Asian-option notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/performance/AsianOptionVarianceReduction.ipynb#Stop-when-the-price-uncertainty-meets-a-tolerance): a price tolerance with drift and a pilot-fitted control

Read each run's [tolerance]{.alert}, estimate, reported interval or bound, sample count, and [decision]{.alert}

::: {.key-point}
Budget exhausted $\ne$ tolerance met

Approximate intervals and conditional bounds need their stated [assumptions]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
The Keister reference is checked only after stopping. The IID interval uses a
pilot-sized final run; the replication interval uses independent scrambles,
not the within-scramble sample variance. Nominal fixed-sample interval coverage
does not automatically carry over to adaptive stopping. Walsh-decay guarantees
assume cone membership, which passing necessary-condition checks cannot prove.
For the Asian option, distinguish simulation error from model and discretization
error, and include the pilot in the computational budget. The linked low
discrepancy constructions notebook compares fixed sample sizes without
duplicating these stopping demonstrations.
:::

## Cost of deterministic low discrepancy sampling {#deterministic-ld-cost .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

<span id="from-error-decay-to-cost"></span>

For fixed cube points write $\hmu_n(h)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}h(\vu_i)$

Recall $D_n(K)=D\bigl(F_{\mathrm{unif}},\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K\bigr)$

For the chosen QMC design, assume a [discrepancy bound]{.alert} $D_n(K)\le a_{\mathrm{QMC}}n^{-p_{\mathrm{QMC}}}$

\begin{align*}
\abs{\mu-\hmu_n(h)}
&\le D_n(K)\operatorname{vtn}_K(h)
\le a_{\mathrm{QMC}}\operatorname{vtn}_K(h)n^{-p_{\mathrm{QMC}}}\\
\text{Choose }n
&\ge
\left(\frac{a_{\mathrm{QMC}}\operatorname{vtn}_K(h)}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/p_{\mathrm{QMC}}}\\
\text{Cost}\qquad C(\varepsilon;h,\mathrm{QMC})
&\lesssim S_{\mathrm{QMC}}(h)+\$_{\mathrm{QMC}}(h)
\left(\frac{a_{\mathrm{QMC}}\operatorname{vtn}_K(h)}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/p_{\mathrm{QMC}}}
\end{align*}

- [Absolute-error]{.alert} target $\varepsilon$; $\lesssim$ allows rounding up to the next design size
- $S_{\mathrm{QMC}}$ is setup; $\$_{\mathrm{QMC}}$ includes point generation and the full $h$ evaluation
- $\operatorname{vtn}_K(h)$ is usually [hard to know or estimate]{.alert}

::: {.notes}
The discrepancy-variation inequality and the assumed discrepancy-rate
upper bound give a sufficient sample size. Choose the smallest allowed
sample size at least as large as the displayed threshold. C denotes the
work needed to meet the specified accuracy; this construction gives an
upper bound on that work, not its unknown exact minimum. The symbol
lesssim absorbs fixed factors from rounding or admissible sample sizes.
It is not an equality or a claim that the realized error attains its bound.
Assume a fixed kernel and domain, h in the associated space,
positive finite variation, a_QMC>0, and p_QMC>0. The zero-variation case
is a constant integrand and needs no asymptotic rate model.
Use the full RKHS norm as variation in general. If constants belong to the
space, these equal-weight averages allow the reduced min_c ||h-c|| variation.

Round up to an admissible sample size and retain logarithmic factors if
they occur in the discrepancy bound. The displayed asymptotic cost assumes
the sample-size threshold is at least one; otherwise retain the one-point
minimum. Allowed sample sizes must have bounded successive ratios for the
rounding factor to be absorbed by lesssim. Cost includes the cube-point generator
and complete integrand evaluation; linear per-point cost is a model.
Use the actual T(n;h) if generating n points has a different cost law.
The chosen QMC construction and its implementation determine a_QMC,
p_QMC, S_QMC(h), and cost_QMC(h); these are not universal QMC constants.
Setup may be explicitly ignored for simple comparisons.

A deterministic estimate has no randomization variance, but that says
nothing about its integration error. The bound requires justified values
or bounds for both discrepancy and variation. Different kernels or scalings
change both factors; compare their product rather than variation alone.
In practice, variation is typically difficult to know or estimate. This is
primarily a theoretical cost comparison, not a directly computable stopping
rule. The preceding stopping section explains error assessments from computed values
and their assumptions; those need not estimate the full variation explicitly.
:::

---

### Cost of randomized low discrepancy sampling {#randomized-ld-cost}

For one unbiased $n$-point run, model the [estimator variance]{.alert} by

$$
\var_{\mathrm{rand}}\{\hmu_n(h)\}
\approx A_{\mathrm{RQMC}}^2(h)n^{-2p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}
$$

\begin{align*}
\operatorname{RMSE}\{\hmu_n(h)\}
&\approx A_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)n^{-p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}\\
\text{For target RMSE }\varepsilon:\quad n
&\approx
\left(\frac{A_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}\\
\text{Cost}\qquad C(\varepsilon;h,\mathrm{RQMC})
&\approx S_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)+\$_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)
\left(\frac{A_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}
\end{align*}

- Predicts work for an [RMSE target]{.alert} $\varepsilon$, averaged over randomizations
- $A_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)$ captures dependence on $h$ and the chosen randomization
- With modest [smoothness]{.alert}, often $p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}>p_{\mathrm{QMC}}$
- The [earlier replication interval](#rqmc-replication-stopping) estimates uncertainty from data

::: {.notes}
The variance is over randomizations of a fixed integrand, and unbiasedness
is assumed. The power law is an approximate model for the chosen integrand,
RQMC construction, randomization, and range of allowed sample sizes.
A_RQMC(h) is its nonnegative error amplitude. It may reflect design-specific
spectral or ANOVA structure and need not factor as a universal method
constant times deterministic RKHS variation. Do not identify it with vtn_K(h).
The squared amplitude is written A_RQMC^2(h), with the square on A.

Unbiasedness makes RMSE squared equal to estimator variance exactly; the
power-law expression for that variance, and the resulting RMSE, sample-size,
and cost formulas, are approximate. They do not assert upper bounds.
Keep p_RQMC distinct from p_QMC. With modest smoothness, randomized
designs often have a larger RMSE decay exponent than the deterministic
error-decay exponent for the corresponding setting. Some smooth integrands under suitable
scrambling admit RMSE nearly n^{-3/2}, but not every integrand or randomization
has that rate. Match the exponent and amplitude to the setting, retaining
logarithmic terms when relevant.

Invert the approximate RMSE law to predict a sample size, then round up to
an admissible size and charge the actual setup and sampling work. Linear
sampling work after setup is a model. A_RQMC(h) is generally unknown, so
this calculation alone does not supply a practical stopping rule. A target
RMSE differs from a deterministic absolute-error guarantee and from a
confidence interval.
:::

---

### Compare low discrepancy costs {#comparing-representations-with-the-same-design}

Compare equal-integral $h_f$ and $h_g$ using the [same design]{.alert} and rate exponent

Omit setup and rounding; for a common tolerance $\varepsilon$, compare

| Method and error criterion | Integrand-dependent factor in leading work |
|:---|:---|
| QMC: absolute-error bound | $\displaystyle\$_{\mathrm{QMC}}(h)\bigl[a_{\mathrm{QMC}}\operatorname{vtn}_K(h)\bigr]^{1/p_{\mathrm{QMC}}}$ |
| RQMC: RMSE model | $\displaystyle\$_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)A_{\mathrm{RQMC}}^{1/p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}(h)$ |

Within each comparison, the common $\varepsilon^{-1/p}$ factor cancels

::: {.key-point}
A smaller [error constant]{.alert} must compensate for greater [cost per point]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
Compare the two representations separately within one method and error
criterion. The QMC row gives a leading work-bound factor; the RQMC row
gives a leading work-model factor. Neither is measured runtime or an unknown
minimum cost. Method, domain, input dimension, exponent, and assumptions
must be compatible. For deterministic QMC, the kernel,
variation definition, and discrepancy-rate constant must also be shared.
Conditioning or a different transformation may change dimension or the
valid rate; then compare the complete method-specific cost expressions instead.

The QMC error amplitude is a_QMC vtn_K(h). The RQMC error amplitude is
A_RQMC(h), which captures the chosen design's estimator-variance behavior.
Do not substitute the deterministic variation for that RQMC quantity.
With a shared exponent p, halving the relevant error amplitude while
doubling per-point cost gives the predicted leading-work ratio 2^{1-1/p}.
It is 1/2 at p=1/2, 1 at p=1, and 2^{1/3} at p=3/2.
Setup and pilot costs may change these finite-tolerance comparisons.

For IID uniform sampling, the RMSE amplitude is sigma(h), p=1/2,
and the factor reduces to cost(h) sigma^2(h). Under RQMC, controls fitted
to minimize IID contribution variance do not automatically minimize
A_RQMC(h) or the variance of a complete randomized estimate.
:::

---

### Comparing IID and RQMC at the same RMSE target {#sd-squared-times-runtime}

Ignore setup; choose $n$ for each method, with [$R$ fixed for RQMC]{.alert}

| Quantity | IID: $\hmu_n$ | RQMC: $\hmu_{R,n}$ |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Variance of one $n$-point estimate | $\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{IID},n}^2=\frac{\sigma^2(h)}n$<br>$\sigma^2(h)=\var\{h(\vU)\}$ | $\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{RQMC},n}^2\approx A_{\mathrm{RQMC}}^2(h)n^{-2p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}$ |
| Variance of the reported estimate | $\displaystyle\frac{\sigma^2(h)}n\approx\frac{\hat\sigma_n^2(h)}n$ | $\displaystyle\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{RQMC},n}^2}R\approx\frac{\hat\sigma_{R,n}^2}R$ |
| Choose $n$ for RMSE $\varepsilon$ | $\displaystyle n\approx\frac{\sigma^2(h)}{\varepsilon^2}$ | $\displaystyle n\approx\left(\frac{A_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)}{\varepsilon\sqrt R}\right)^{1/p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}$ |
| Work | $\displaystyle\approx\frac{\$_{\mathrm{IID}}(h)\sigma^2(h)}{\varepsilon^2}$ | $\displaystyle\approx\frac{\$_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)A_{\mathrm{RQMC}}^{1/p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}(h)R^{1-1/(2p_{\mathrm{RQMC}})}}{\varepsilon^{1/p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}}$ |

Work: $n\$_{\mathrm{IID}}(h)$ for IID; $Rn\$_{\mathrm{RQMC}}(h)$ for RQMC

::: {.key-point}
Work scales as $\varepsilon^{-2}$ for IID; $\varepsilon^{-1/p_{\mathrm{RQMC}}}$ for RQMC with [fixed $R$]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
Compare unbiased estimates of the same target integral, using the same cube
integrand h. For IID sampling, sigma^2(h)=var{h(U)} is the finite variance of
one function value. Independence gives the variance of an n-point average
as sigma_IID,n^2=sigma^2(h)/n. This one-value variance is defined in the IID
column because the RQMC model uses the variance of the complete design.
For RQMC, sigma_RQMC,n^2 is the randomization variance of the entire n-point
estimate, modeled approximately by A_RQMC^2(h)n^{-2p_RQMC}. The points
within a run are dependent; independent randomizations give independent
complete run estimates.

The reported-variance row pairs each population variance with its sample
estimate. For IID, hat sigma_n^2(h) is the ordinary sample variance of the
n individual function values, with denominator n-1:
$\hat\sigma_n^2(h)=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}[h(\vU_i)-\hmu_n]^2$.
Divide by n to estimate the variance of their average. For RQMC,
hat sigma_{R,n}^2 is the across-run sample variance of the R independent
n-point averages, with denominator R-1, defined on the replication slide.
Divide by R to estimate the variance of their reported average. These
approximation signs indicate estimated variances, not error bounds or a
claim of exact agreement with the population variances.

IID reports one average of n independent function values, with no replication
count R. Its variance is sigma^2(h)/n, so choosing n approximately
sigma^2(h)/epsilon^2 targets RMSE epsilon.
For RQMC, fix R in advance and average R independently randomized n-point
run estimates. Their mean has variance equal to the complete-run variance
divided by R. Equating this to epsilon^2 gives n approximately
[A_RQMC(h)/(epsilon sqrt(R))]^{1/p_RQMC}. Choose n separately for each method.

Ignore setup and assume linear work: n times the IID per-point cost, and
Rn times the RQMC per-point cost. Each cost includes point generation and
the complete h evaluation. Substituting the chosen n gives the last row.
IID work is approximately cost_IID(h) sigma^2(h) epsilon^{-2}.
RQMC work is approximately
cost_RQMC(h) A_RQMC^{1/p_RQMC}(h)
R^{1-1/(2p_RQMC)} epsilon^{-1/p_RQMC}.
Both costs are approximations: the model ignores rounding and setup, and
the RQMC variance rate is itself approximate. For p_RQMC>1/2, more replications
increase predicted work at a common RMSE because they require more total
points. At p_RQMC=1/2 the R factor cancels, as for an IID rate.

Round n up to an admissible size and retain at least one point per run.
The asymptotic work formulas apply when the predicted n is at least one
and within the rate model's valid range. Retain logarithmic factors or
nonlinear generation costs when present. A_RQMC(h) and its valid rate may
be unknown, so these formulas plan theoretical work; they are not a practical
stopping rule or a confidence-coverage claim.

This comparison increases n as the requested RMSE decreases, keeping the
RQMC replication count R fixed. The IID calculation uses one sample average
throughout. Holding the RQMC design size n fixed and only increasing R would
give an epsilon^{-2} replication work law; that is a different allocation.

The notebook timings charge actual work. Each controlled Asian-option run
regenerates an independent pilot, so its measured runtime includes that
pilot even though this simple table omits setup. If another design reuses
one fitted control, analyze residual variance conditional on that pilot and
charge its setup once; unconditional run estimates need not be independent.
The comparison concerns the same discretely monitored contract; model or
discretization bias is separate.
[Asian/lookback comparison](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/performance/AsianOptionVarianceReduction.ipynb).
:::

### Worked cost comparison: IID versus RQMC {#iid-rqmc-cost-example}

Assume unbiased estimates, equal [cost per point]{.alert}, and no setup cost<br>
Let $\var\{h(\vU)\}=1$ and, for [large $n$]{.alert}, model one RQMC run by $\sigma_n^2\approx16/n^2$

Fix $R=16$ independent RQMC replications and target [RMSE]{.alert} $\varepsilon=0.01$

$$
\operatorname{MSE}(\hmu_N^{\mathrm{IID}})=\frac1N
\qquad
\operatorname{MSE}(\hmu_{16,n})=\frac{\sigma_n^2}{16}\approx\frac1{n^2}
$$

| | IID | RQMC |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Required size | $N=10{,}000$ | $n\ge100$ per run |
| Chosen size | $N=10{,}000$ | $n=128$ per run |
| Total point evaluations | $10{,}000$ | $16\times128=2{,}048$ |
| RMSE | $0.01$ | $\approx1/128=0.0078125$ |

Round RQMC up to a [power of two]{.alert}

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>For ten times smaller RMSE, how does each method's work grow before rounding?</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a hypothetical planning example, not a measured speed comparison.
The two methods integrate the same fixed h with variance one under uniform
inputs. Assume the RQMC variance model holds at the design sizes used here;
it is not asserted for every n or every integrand. In particular, the law
16/n^2 need not apply at very small n. With the earlier notation,
A_RQMC(h)=4 and p_RQMC=1. Sixteen independent randomizations give the
reported mean variance sigma_n^2/16, approximately 1/n^2.

IID needs N >= epsilon^{-2}; choose the integer N=10,000. RQMC needs
n approximately at least epsilon^{-1}=100, then rounds up to n=128 for
the selected power-of-two design. Total RQMC work is Rn=2,048 evaluations,
versus 10,000 for IID. Equal per-point costs and omitted overhead make
evaluation counts proportional to runtime in this example. Actual sequence
generation, setup, error assessment, and pilot costs can change the comparison.

For epsilon=0.001, IID needs 1,000,000 evaluations, a factor 100 more.
Before rounding, RQMC needs n=1,000 per run and 16,000 evaluations,
a factor 10 more than its unrounded 1,600-evaluation work at epsilon=0.01.
After power-of-two rounding, use n=1,024 and 16,384 evaluations, eight
times the rounded 2,048-evaluation work in the table. Distinguish the rate
comparison before rounding from the realized design-size ratios.

The RQMC variance law is an assumed model; a small pilot does not establish
it. Meeting the modeled RMSE target is not a confidence-coverage guarantee
or a justified adaptive stopping rule. These are the separate qualifications
developed under Stopping criteria.

At n=1, each randomized run is one uniform draw, so sigma_1^2=1 exactly.
Sixteen independent replications are then exactly the same estimator as
IID with N=16, with MSE 1/16. Extrapolating the large-n model would give
sigma_1^2 approximately 16 and reported-mean MSE approximately 1, which
is wrong. This is why the large-n qualification is explicit on the slide.
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder" .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-low-discrepancy"}

- Equivalent [expectations]{.alert} can have dramatically different computational [variance]{.alert}
- Exact transport chooses a map that makes the target-to-proposal correction
  [constant]{.alert}<br>Importance sampling retains the correction as [unequal]{.alert} weights
- Importance proposals may be [tailored]{.alert} to a particular integrand<br>Transported
  target samples can be [reused]{.alert} for many integrands
- Self-normalized IS cancels unknown density [scale]{.alert}<br>Its ratio is consistent under suitable conditions, but generally [biased]{.alert} at finite $n$

## Big Ideas (continued) {data-state="goldborder"}

- Control variates and conditioning remove variability using [known]{.alert} structure
- Antithetic sampling and Latin hypercubes introduce useful [dependence]{.alert} deliberately
- Low discrepancy sequences replace random [clustering]{.alert} with [balanced]{.alert} space filling
- Randomization restores [unbiasedness]{.alert} and supports error estimation while retaining QMC efficiency

# How Far We Have Come

From a [simulation model]{.alert} to an [accurate answer at an affordable cost]{.alert}

- [Formulate]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#moments-of-random-variables) — expectations, probabilities, quantiles, and sampling uncertainty<br>[Travel time]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#are-we-there-yet-revisited): translate a practical question into a simulation output
- [Generate]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#from-uniformity-to-a-target-distribution) — transform uniform inputs into dependent vectors and paths<br>[Option pricing]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#option-payoffs-and-prices): simulate stock paths and average discounted payoffs
- [Extend]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#the-metropolishastings-algorithm) — use MCMC when direct target sampling is difficult<br>[Bayesian inference]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#bayesian-inference): estimate posterior summaries without the target normalizer
- [Simulate]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#queueing-systems) — advance a system using its current state and next event<br>[Queueing]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#queueing-systems): estimate customer time and blocking
- [Improve the representation](#variance-and-variation-reduction) — importance weights, controls, and conditioning<br>[Asian options](#combining-efficiency-methods): combine methods while preserving the desired expectation
- [Design and assess](#randomized-low-discrepancy-sampling) — structured points; discrepancy bounds or independent RQMC replications<br>[Stopping](#stopping-criteria) and [cost](#deterministic-ld-cost): justify accuracy and compare work at the same tolerance

::: {.key-point}
Choose the [representation]{.alert} and [point design]{.alert} for [accuracy per unit of work]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a cumulative course recap rather than another list of Deck 04 methods.
Introduction supplied the statistical questions and error vocabulary;
Generating Samples supplied transforms, dependence, paths, and payoffs;
Markov Chain Monte Carlo supplied invariant-target sampling, event-driven
systems, and kernel discrepancy. Improving Efficiency changes the
representation of the integral and the design of its uniform inputs, then
asks how to assess error and compare total work at the desired accuracy.

The roles remain f(X), g(Z), and h(U). Equal expectations do not imply equal
output distributions. Self-normalized IS is a ratio extension and generally
has finite-sample bias; the fixed-contribution variance formulas do not
automatically cover it. Independent RQMC replications estimate uncertainty
over randomizations, whereas a single fixed design needs suitable analytic
or model-based error assessment. Keep the separate stopping-coverage
qualifications and include setup and pilots when comparing actual work.
:::

# Choose the Method for the Task {data-state="goldborder"}

- [Task]{.alert}: generate samples $\vX_i$, evaluate contributions $Y_i$, assess error
- [Cost–benefit]{.alert}: compare total work for the required accuracy
    - Setup
    - Pilots
    - Generation
    - Transforms
    - Weights
    - Evaluation
- [Use]{.alert}
    - Mean requires the correct [expectation]{.alert}
    - Density, probability, or quantile requires the appropriate [distributional]{.alert} calculation


::: {.key-point}
Additional machinery must [earn its cost]{.alert}<br>
Choose the complete method by [accuracy per unit of work]{.alert}, for the intended output
:::

::: {.notes}
The gamma convention here is shape k and rate lambda; the sum-of-exponentials
construction requires a positive integer shape. The quantile construction uses
one uniform input and a generally numerical inverse CDF, whereas the sum uses
k independent uniforms and k logarithms. Benchmark the actual implementations
rather than assuming either is faster. For IID draws the two constructions
produce the same target law and hence the same distribution of f(X), assuming
exact transforms; their costs differ. With low discrepancy inputs, dimension
and smoothness also affect integration error.

Define the desired output before choosing a method. For an unbiased IID mean
estimator with finite variance and per-contribution cost c, ignoring setup,
work to reach RMSE epsilon is approximately c var(Y)/epsilon^2. Include setup,
pilot fitting, sampling, transformations, and evaluation in the actual budget.
A variance reduction alone does not establish an overall efficiency gain;
compare complete estimators at the required accuracy. Dependent designs,
adaptive stopping, density estimation, and quantiles require their appropriate
error assessment, not an automatic substitution into this IID formula.

Probability is itself an expectation of an indicator, so one does not always
need unweighted target draws to estimate it. Importance weights can estimate
probabilities and CDFs; an appropriately normalized weighted empirical CDF can
be inverted for quantiles. Conditional methods can estimate probabilities and
densities directly, as the Asian example shows. These methods need valid
weights or conditional formulas for the requested distributional quantity.
A control-adjusted or weighted scalar contribution with the correct mean does
not generally have the original output distribution; do not use its raw
histogram or quantiles as those of the original output. If reusable unweighted
target samples are required, choose a method that actually produces them.
:::
